Come and listen, all you+ who fear God, and I will declare what He has done for my soul. - Psalm 66:16

Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible, kept closer to the author’s own Bible where his argument rests on its wording; capitals for God in quotations (He, His) follow the BSB. “You+” marks every plural “you” (the older “ye”); a plain “you” is singular or general.

A Preface, or Brief Account of the Publishing of This Work

Written by its author, and dedicated to those whom God has counted him worthy to beget to faith by his ministry in the word

Children, grace be with you+, Amen. I am taken from you+ in presence, and so tied up that I cannot perform the duty that lies on me from God toward you+, for your+ further edifying and building up in faith and holiness, etc. Yet, so that you+ may see that my soul has a fatherly care and desire for your+ spiritual and everlasting welfare, I now once again, as before from the top of Shenir and Hermon, so now from the lions’ dens and from the mountains of the leopards (S. of Song 4:8), still look after you+ all, greatly longing to see your+ safe arrival into the desired haven.

I thank God upon every remembrance of you+, and rejoice, even while I stick between the teeth of the lions in the wilderness, at the grace, and mercy, and knowledge of Christ our Savior, which God has bestowed on you+, with abundance of faith and love. Your+ hungerings and thirstings also after further acquaintance with the Father, in His Son, your+ tenderness of heart, your+ trembling at sin, your+ sober and holy conduct also, before both God and men, are a great refreshment to me: “For you+ are my glory and joy” (1 Thess 2:20).

I have sent you+ here enclosed a drop of that honey that I have taken out of the carcass of a lion (Judg 14:5–9). I have eaten of it myself also, and am much refreshed by it. (Temptations, when we first meet them, are like the lion that roared at Samson; but if we overcome them, the next time we see them we shall find a nest of honey within them.) The Philistines do not understand me. It is something of a relation of the work of God upon my soul, from the very first till now, in which you+ may perceive my castings down and risings up; for he wounds, and his hands make whole. It is written in the Scripture (Isa 38:19), “The father will make known the truth of God to the children.” Indeed, it was for this reason that I lay so long at Sinai (Deut 4:10, 11), to see the fire, and the cloud, and the darkness, that I might fear the Lord all the days of my life on earth, and tell of his wondrous works to my children (Ps 78:3–5).

Moses (Num 33:1, 2) wrote of the journeyings of the children of Israel from Egypt to the land of Canaan, and commanded also that they should remember their forty years’ travel in the wilderness: “Remember that these forty years the Lord your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart, whether or not you would keep His commandments” (Deut 8:2). So this I have endeavored to do; and not only that, but to publish it also, so that, if God wills, others may be put in remembrance of what He has done for their souls, by reading His work upon me.

It is profitable for Christians to be often calling to mind the very beginnings of grace in their souls. “Because the Lord kept a vigil that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt, this same night is to be a vigil to the Lord, to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come” (Exod 12:42). “My God,” says David (Ps 42:6), “my soul is cast down within me; but I will remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon, from the hill Mizar.” He remembered also the lion and the bear when he went to fight with the giant of Gath (1 Sam 17:36, 37).

It was Paul’s accustomed manner (Acts 22), and that when he was tried for his life (Acts 24), to open, even before his judges, the manner of his conversion: he would think of that day and that hour in which he first met with grace, for he found it supported him. When God had brought the children of Israel out of the Red Sea, far into the wilderness, yet they had to turn quite about to it again, to remember the drowning of their enemies there (Num 14:25). For though they sang His praise before, yet “they soon forgot His works” (Ps 106:11–13).

In this discourse of mine you+ may see much; much, I say, of the grace of God toward me. I thank God I can count it much, for it was above my sins and Satan’s temptations too. I can remember my fears, and doubts, and sad months with comfort; they are as the head of Goliath in my hand. There was nothing to David like Goliath’s sword, that very sword that should have been sheathed in his own bowels; for the very sight and remembrance of it preached God’s deliverance to him. Oh, the remembrance of my great sins, of my great temptations, and of my great fears of perishing forever! They bring fresh into my mind the remembrance of my great help, my great support from heaven, and the great grace that God extended to such a wretch as I.

My dear children, call to mind the former days and the years of ancient times; remember also your+ songs in the night; and commune with your+ own hearts (Ps 77:5–12). Indeed, look diligently, and leave no corner in them unsearched, for there is treasure hidden there, even the treasure of your+ first and second experience of the grace of God toward you+. Remember, I say, the word that first laid hold upon you+; remember your+ terrors of conscience, and fear of death and hell; remember also your+ tears and prayers to God; yes, how you+ sighed under every hedge for mercy. Have you+ no hill Mizar to remember? Have you+ forgotten the field, the milk house, the stable, the barn, and the like, where God visited your+ souls? Remember also the Word—the Word, I say, upon which the Lord has caused you+ to hope. If you+ have sinned against light; if you+ are tempted to blaspheme; if you+ are down in despair; if you+ think God fights against you+; or if heaven is hidden from your+ eyes, remember it was so with your+ father, “but out of them all the Lord delivered me.”

I could have enlarged much in this discourse of mine on my temptations and troubles for sin, as also on the merciful kindness and working of God with my soul. I could also have stepped into a style much higher than this in which I have here written, and could have adorned all things more than I have here seemed to do, but I dare not. God did not play in convicting me, the devil did not play in tempting me, neither did I play when I sank as into a bottomless pit, when “the pangs of hell caught hold upon me”; so I must not play in relating them, but must be plain and simple, and lay down the thing as it was. He who likes it, let him receive it; and he who does not, let him produce a better. Farewell.

My dear children, the milk and honey is beyond this wilderness. God be merciful to you+, and grant that you+ may not be slothful to go in to possess the land.

Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners

1. In this my relation of the merciful working of God upon my soul, it will not be amiss if, in the first place, I give you, in a few words, a hint of my pedigree and manner of bringing up; so that by this the goodness and bounty of God toward me may be the more exalted and magnified before the sons of men.

2. For my descent, then, it was, as is well known by many, of a low and inconsiderable family, my father’s house being of that rank that is lowliest and most despised of all the families in the land. So I have nothing here, as others have, to boast of in noble blood or a high-born state according to the flesh; though, all things considered, I magnify the heavenly Majesty for this, that by this door He brought me into this world, to partake of the grace and life that is in Christ by the gospel.

3. But yet, notwithstanding the lowliness and inconsiderableness of my parents, it pleased God to put it into their hearts to put me to school, to learn both to read and to write; which I also attained, much as other poor men’s children did; though, to my shame I confess, I soon lost that little I learned, even almost utterly, and that long before the Lord worked His gracious work of conversion upon my soul.

4. As for my own natural life, for the time that I was without God in the world, it was indeed in keeping with “the ways of this world” and with “the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience” (Eph 2:2, 3). It was my delight to be one whom the devil “has taken captive to his will” (2 Tim 2:26). I was filled with all unrighteousness, which also worked and put itself forth so strongly, both in my heart and life, and that from a child, that I had but few equals, especially considering my years, which were tender, being few, both for cursing, swearing, lying, and blaspheming the holy name of God.

5. Indeed, I was so settled and rooted in these things that they became like a second nature to me; and this, as I have also soberly considered since, so offended the Lord that even in my childhood He scared and frightened me with fearful dreams, and terrified me with dreadful visions. For often, after I had spent this and that day in sin, I have been greatly afflicted in my bed, while asleep, with the sense of devils and wicked spirits, who continually, as I then thought, labored to draw me away with them, of which I could never be rid.

6. Also at these years I would be greatly afflicted and troubled with the thoughts of the day of judgment, and that both night and day, and would tremble at the thoughts of the fearful torments of hellfire; always fearing that it would be my lot to be found at last among those devils and hellish fiends who are bound down there with the chains and bonds of darkness, “for judgment on that great day.”

7. These things, I say, when I was but a child about nine or ten years old, so distressed my soul that then, in the midst of my many sports and childish vanities, amid my vain companions, I was often much cast down and afflicted in my mind by them; yet I could not let go of my sins. Indeed, I was also then so overcome with despair of life and heaven that I would often wish either that there had been no hell, or that I had been a devil, supposing they were only tormentors; so that if I indeed had to go there, I might be a tormentor rather than be tormented myself.

8. A while after, these terrible dreams left me, and I also soon forgot them; for my pleasures quickly cut off the remembrance of them, as if they had never been. So, with more greediness, according to the strength of nature, I continued to let loose the reins to my lust, and delighted in all transgression against the law of God; so that, until I came to the state of marriage, I was the very ringleader of all the youth that kept me company, in all manner of vice and ungodliness.

9. Indeed, the lusts and fruits of the flesh had such power in this poor soul of mine that, had not a miracle of precious grace prevented it, I would not only have perished by the stroke of eternal justice, but would also have laid myself open even to the stroke of those laws which bring some to disgrace and open shame before the face of the world.

10. In these days the thoughts of religion were very grievous to me; I could neither endure it myself, nor endure that any other should; so that, when I saw some reading in those books that concerned Christian piety, it would be as it were a prison to me. Then I said to God, “Depart from me! For I have no desire to know Your ways” (Job 21:14). I was now void of all good consideration; heaven and hell were both out of sight and mind; and as for saving and damning, they were least in my thoughts. O Lord, You know my life, and my ways were not hidden from You.

11. But this I well remember: though I could myself sin with the greatest delight and ease, and also take pleasure in the vileness of my companions, yet even then, if I at any time saw wicked things done by those who professed goodness, it would make my spirit tremble. As once, above all the rest, when I was at the height of my vanity, I heard one swear who was reckoned a religious man, and it struck my spirit so greatly that it made my heart ache.

12. But God did not utterly leave me, but followed me still, not now with convictions of sin, but with judgments; yet such as were mixed with mercy. For once I fell into a creek of the sea, and hardly escaped drowning. Another time I fell out of a boat into Bedford river, but mercy still preserved me alive. Besides, another time, being in the field with one of my companions, it happened that an adder crossed the highway; so I, having a stick in my hand, struck her over the back; and having stunned her, I forced open her mouth with my stick and plucked her sting out with my fingers; by which act, had not God been merciful to me, I might, by my desperateness, have brought myself to my end.

13. This also I have taken notice of with thanksgiving: when I was a soldier, I, with others, was drawn out to go to a certain place to besiege it; but when I was just ready to go, one of the company asked to go in my place; and when I had consented, he took my place, and coming to the siege, as he stood sentinel, he was shot in the head with a musket bullet, and died.

14. Here, as I said, were judgments and mercy, but neither of them awakened my soul to righteousness; so I sinned still, and grew more and more rebellious against God, and careless of my own salvation.

15. Soon after this I changed my condition into a married state, and my mercy was to find a wife whose father was counted godly. This woman and I, though we came together as poor as poor could be, not having so much household stuff as a dish or spoon between us both, yet she had this for her part, The Plain Man’s Pathway to Heaven and The Practice of Piety, which her father had left her when he died. In these two books I would sometimes read with her, and in them I also found some things that were somewhat pleasing to me; but all this while I met with no conviction. She also would often be telling me what a godly man her father was, and how he would reprove and correct vice, both in his house and among his neighbors; what a strict and holy life he lived in his day, both in word and deed.

16. So these books, with this account, though they did not reach my heart to awaken it about my sad and sinful state, yet they did beget within me some desires for religion; so that, because I knew no better, I fell in very eagerly with the religion of the times: that is, to go to church twice a day, and that too with the foremost, and there very devoutly both say and sing as others did, yet keeping my wicked life. But with that, I was so overrun with the spirit of superstition that I adored, and that with great devotion, even all things, both the high place, priest, clerk, vestments, service, and whatever else belonged to the church; counting all things holy that were contained in it, and especially the priest and clerk most happy and, without doubt, greatly blessed, because they were the servants, as I then thought, of God, and were principal in the holy temple, to do His work in it.

17. This notion grew so strong upon my spirit in a little time that, had I but seen a priest, however sordid and debauched in his life, I would find my spirit fall under him, reverence him, and be knit to him. Indeed, I thought that, for the love I bore them, supposing they were the ministers of God, I could have lain down at their feet and been trampled on by them; their name, their garb, and their work so intoxicated and bewitched me.

18. After I had been like this for some considerable time, another thought came into my mind; and that was, whether we were of the Israelites or not. For, finding in the Scriptures that they were once the special people of God, I thought, if only I were of this race, my soul must surely be happy. Now again I found within me a great longing to be satisfied about this question, but could not tell how I should be. At last I asked my father about it, who told me, No, we were not. So then my spirit fell as to the hopes of that, and so remained.

19. But all this while I was not aware of the danger and evil of sin; I was kept from considering that sin would damn me, whatever religion I followed, unless I was found in Christ. No, I never thought of Him, nor whether there was such a one or not. Thus man, while blind, wanders, but wearies himself with vanity, for he does not know the way to the city of God (Eccl 10:15).

20. But one day, among all the sermons our parson preached, his subject was the Sabbath day, and the evil of breaking it, whether with labor, sports, or otherwise. Now I was, notwithstanding my religion, one who took much delight in all manner of vice, and that was especially the day on which I indulged myself in it. So I fell in my conscience under his sermon, thinking and believing that he made that sermon on purpose to show me my evil doing; and at that time I felt what guilt was, though never before, that I can remember; but then I was, for the present, greatly loaded with it, and so went home when the sermon was ended with a great burden on my spirit.

21. This, for that instant, numbed the sinews of my best delights, and embittered my former pleasures to me; but behold, it did not last, for before I had well dined, the trouble began to go off my mind, and my heart returned to its old course. But oh, how glad I was that this trouble was gone from me, and that the fire was put out, so that I might sin again without control! So, when I had satisfied nature with my food, I shook the sermon out of my mind, and returned with great delight to my old custom of sports and gaming.

22. But the same day, as I was in the midst of a game of cat, and having struck it one blow from the hole, just as I was about to strike it the second time, a voice suddenly darted from heaven into my soul, which said, “Will you leave your sins and go to heaven, or have your sins and go to hell?” At this I was put into an exceeding amazement; so, leaving my cat on the ground, I looked up to heaven, and it was as if I had, with the eyes of my understanding, seen the Lord Jesus looking down upon me, as being very hotly displeased with me, and as if He severely threatened me with some grievous punishment for these and my other ungodly practices.

23. I had no sooner conceived this in my mind than suddenly this conclusion was fastened on my spirit (for the former hint set my sins again before my face), that I had been a great and grievous sinner, and that it was now too late for me to look after heaven; for Christ would not forgive me, nor pardon my transgressions. Then I fell to musing upon this also; and while I was thinking of it, and fearing lest it should be so, I felt my heart sink in despair, concluding it was too late; and therefore I resolved in my mind that I would go on in sin. For, I thought, if the case is so, my state is surely miserable: miserable if I leave my sins, and only miserable if I follow them; I can only be damned, and if it must be so, I might as well be damned for many sins as be damned for few.

24. Thus I stood in the midst of my play, before all who were then present; yet I told them nothing. But, I say, having made this conclusion, I returned desperately to my sport again; and I well remember that at once this kind of despair so possessed my soul that I was persuaded I could never attain any other comfort than what I should get in sin; for heaven was gone already, so that I must not think of that. So I found within me a great desire to take my fill of sin, continually scheming what sin was yet to be committed, that I might taste the sweetness of it; and I made as much haste as I could to fill my belly with its delicacies, lest I should die before I had my desire; for that I feared greatly. In these things, I declare before God, I do not lie, nor do I feign this form of speech; these were really, strongly, and with all my heart my desires. The good Lord, whose mercy is unsearchable, forgive me my transgressions.

25. And I am very confident that this temptation of the devil is more usual among poor creatures than many are aware of: to overrun their spirits with a scurvy and seared frame of heart, and a benumbing of conscience; which frame he quietly and slyly supplies with such despair that, though not much guilt attends their souls, yet they continually have a secret conclusion within them that there is no hope for them; for they have loved sins, “therefore after them they will go” (Jer 2:25; 18:12).

26. Now therefore I went on in sin with great greediness of mind, continually grudging that I could not be as satisfied with it as I would have liked. This continued with me about a month or more. But one day, as I was standing at a neighbor’s shop window, and there cursing and swearing and playing the madman after my usual manner, the woman of the house sat within and heard me. Though she also was a very loose and ungodly wretch, yet she declared that I swore and cursed at such a most fearful rate that she was made to tremble to hear me; and she told me further that I was the ungodliest fellow for swearing that she had ever heard in all her life, and that I, by doing this, was able to spoil all the youth in the whole town, if they but came into my company.

27. At this reproof I was silenced, and put to secret shame, and that too, as I thought, before the God of heaven. So, while I stood there hanging down my head, I wished with all my heart that I might be a little child again, that my father might teach me to speak without this wicked way of swearing; for, I thought, I am so accustomed to it that it is but in vain for me to think of a reformation, for I thought it could never be.

28. But how it came to pass I do not know: from this time forward I so left my swearing that it was a great wonder to myself to observe it; and whereas before I did not know how to speak unless I put an oath before and another behind, to make my words have authority, now I could speak better without it, and with more pleasantness, than ever I could before. All this while I did not know Jesus Christ, nor did I leave my sports and play.

29. But quickly after this I fell into company with a poor man who made profession of religion, who, as I then thought, talked pleasantly of the Scriptures and of the matters of religion. So, falling into some love and liking for what he said, I took myself to my Bible, and began to take great pleasure in reading, but especially in the historical part of it; for as for Paul’s epistles and such Scriptures, I could not bear them, being as yet ignorant either of the corruptions of my nature, or of my need of Jesus Christ and His worth to save me.

30. So I fell to some outward reformation, both in my words and life, and set the commandments before me as my way to heaven; and I also strove to keep these commandments, and, as I thought, kept them pretty well at times, and then I would have comfort; yet now and then I would break one, and so afflict my conscience; but then I would repent, and say I was sorry for it, and promise God to do better next time, and there get help again; for then I thought I pleased God as well as any man in England.

31. Thus I continued about a year, all which time our neighbors took me to be a very godly man, a new and religious man, and marveled much to see such a great and famous alteration in my life and conduct; and indeed so it was, though I did not yet know Christ, nor grace, nor faith, nor hope; for, as I have clearly seen since, had I then died, my state would have been most fearful. Well, this, I say, continued about a twelvemonth or more.

32. But, I say, my neighbors were amazed at this great conversion of mine, from prodigious profaneness to something like a moral life; and truly, so they well might be; for this conversion of mine was as great as for Tom of Bedlam to become a sober man. Now, therefore, they began to praise, to commend, and to speak well of me, both to my face and behind my back. Now, as they said, I had become godly; now I had become a truly upright man. But oh! when I understood that these were their words and opinions of me, it pleased me mighty well. For though as yet I was nothing but a poor painted hypocrite, yet I loved to be talked of as one who was truly godly. I was proud of my godliness, and indeed I did all I did either to be seen by men or to be well spoken of by them. And thus I continued for about a twelvemonth or more.

33. Now you must know that before this I had taken much delight in ringing the bells; but my conscience beginning to be tender, I thought such practice was but vain, and therefore forced myself to leave it; yet my mind hankered, so I would go to the steeple-house and look on, though I dared not ring. But I thought this did not become religion either; yet I forced myself, and would still look on. But quickly after, I began to think, “What if one of the bells should fall?” Then I chose to stand under a main beam that lay across the steeple from side to side, thinking I might stand safe there; but then I would think again: should the bell fall with a swing, it might first hit the wall, and then, rebounding upon me, might kill me in spite of this beam. This made me stand in the steeple door; and now, I thought, I am safe enough; for if a bell should then fall, I can slip out behind these thick walls, and so be preserved notwithstanding.

34. So after this I would still go to see them ring, but would not go further than the steeple door; but then it came into my head, “What if the steeple itself should fall?” And this thought, “It may fall, for all I know,” when I stood and looked on, so continually shook my mind that I dared not stand at the steeple door any longer, but was forced to flee, for fear the steeple should fall upon my head.

35. Another thing was my dancing: I was a full year before I could quite leave that. But all this while, when I thought I kept this or that commandment, or did by word or deed anything that I thought was good, I had great peace in my conscience, and would think to myself, “God cannot help but be pleased with me now”; indeed, to tell it in my own way, I thought no man in England could please God better than I.

36. But, poor wretch as I was, I was all this while ignorant of Jesus Christ, and going about to establish my own righteousness; and I would have perished in it, had not God in mercy shown me more of my state by nature.

37. But one day the good providence of God cast me to Bedford, to work at my calling; and in one of the streets of that town I came where there were three or four poor women sitting at a door in the sun, talking about the things of God. And being now willing to hear them talk, I drew near to hear what they said, for I was now a lively talker myself in the matters of religion; but I may say, I heard, but I did not understand; for they were far above, out of my reach. Their talk was about a new birth, the work of God on their hearts, also how they were convicted of their miserable state by nature; they talked of how God had visited their souls with His love in the Lord Jesus, and with what words and promises they had been refreshed, comforted, and supported against the temptations of the devil. Moreover, they reasoned of the suggestions and temptations of Satan in particular, and told one another by which of them they had been afflicted, and how they were borne up under his assaults. They also discussed their own wretchedness of heart and their unbelief, and did despise, slight, and abhor their own righteousness, as filthy and insufficient to do them any good.

38. And it seemed to me they spoke as if joy made them speak; they spoke with such pleasantness of Scripture language, and with such an appearance of grace in all they said, that they were to me as if they had found a new world, as if they were people who dwelt alone, and were not to be reckoned among their neighbors (Num 23:9).

39. At this I felt my own heart begin to shake, and to suspect that my condition was bad; for I saw that in all my thoughts about religion and salvation, the new birth never entered my mind; neither did I know the comfort of the Word and promise, nor the deceitfulness and treachery of my own wicked heart. As for secret thoughts, I took no notice of them; neither did I understand what Satan’s temptations were, nor how they were to be withstood and resisted, etc.

40. Thus, therefore, when I had heard and considered what they said, I left them and went about my work again; but their talk and discourse went with me; also my heart would stay with them, for I was greatly affected by their words, both because by them I was convinced that I lacked the true marks of a truly godly man, and also because by them I was convinced of the happy and blessed condition of him who was such a one.

41. Therefore I would often make it my business to go again and again into the company of these poor people, for I could not stay away; and the more I went among them, the more I questioned my condition. And as I still remember, I at once found two things within me, at which I at times marveled, especially considering what a blind, ignorant, sordid, and ungodly wretch I had been just before: the one was a very great softness and tenderness of heart, which caused me to fall under the conviction of what they asserted from Scripture; and the other was a great bending in my mind to a continual meditating on them, and on all other good things which at any time I heard or read of.

42. By these things my mind was now so turned that it lay like a horseleech at the vein, continually crying out, “Give, give” (Prov 30:15). Indeed, it was so fixed on eternity, and on the things about the kingdom of heaven (that is, so far as I knew, though as yet, God knows, I knew but little), that neither pleasures nor profits, nor persuasions nor threats, could loosen it or make it let go its hold. And though I may say it with shame, yet it is in very deed a certain truth: it would then have been as difficult for me to take my mind from heaven to earth as I have often found it since to get it again from earth to heaven.

43. One thing I must not omit. There was a young man in our town to whom my heart had before been knit more than to any other; but he being a most wicked creature for cursing, and swearing, and whoring, I now shook him off and forsook his company. But about a quarter of a year after I had left him, I met him in a certain lane and asked him how he was; he, after his old swearing and mad way, answered that he was well. “But, Harry,” said I, “why do you swear and curse like this? What will become of you if you die in this condition?” He answered me in a great rage, “What would the devil do for company, if it were not for such as I am?”

44. About this time I met with some Ranters’ books, put out by some of our countrymen, which books were also highly esteemed by several old professing Christians. Some of these I read, but was not able to make a judgment about them; so, as I read in them and thought upon them, feeling myself unable to judge, I would betake myself to hearty prayer in this manner: “O Lord, I am a fool, and not able to know the truth from error. Lord, do not leave me to my own blindness, either to approve of or condemn this doctrine; if it is of God, let me not despise it; if it is of the devil, let me not embrace it. Lord, I lay my soul in this matter only at Your foot; let me not be deceived, I humbly beseech You.” I had one religious intimate companion all this while, and that was the poor man I spoke of before; but about this time he also turned a most devilish Ranter, and gave himself up to all manner of filthiness, especially uncleanness. He would also deny that there was a God, angel, or spirit, and would laugh at all exhortations to sobriety. When I labored to rebuke his wickedness, he would laugh the more, and claim that he had gone through all religions and could never hit on the right one till now. He told me also that in a little time I should see all professing Christians turn to the ways of the Ranters. So, abhorring those cursed principles, I left his company immediately, and became as great a stranger to him as I had been a familiar friend before.

45. Nor was this man alone a temptation to me; but, my calling lying in the country, I happened to fall into the company of several people who, though strict in religion formerly, were also swept away by these Ranters. These would also talk with me of their ways, and condemn me as legalistic and dark, claiming that only those had attained to perfection who could do what they would and not sin. Oh! these temptations were suited to my flesh, I being but a young man, and my nature in its prime; but God, who had, as I hope, designed me for better things, kept me in the fear of His name, and did not allow me to accept such cursed principles. And blessed be God, who put it into my heart to cry to Him to be kept and directed, always distrusting my own wisdom; for I have since seen the very effect of that prayer, in His preserving me not only from the Ranters’ errors, but also from those that have sprung up since. The Bible was precious to me in those days.

46. And now, it seemed to me, I began to look into the Bible with new eyes, and read as I never did before; and especially the epistles of the apostle St. Paul were sweet and pleasant to me. And indeed I was then never out of the Bible, either by reading or meditation, continually crying out to God that I might know the truth and the way to heaven and glory.

47. And as I went on and read, I came upon that passage, “To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit, to another faith,” etc. (1 Cor 12:8, 9). And though, as I have since seen, by this Scripture the Holy Spirit intends especially things extraordinary, yet on me it then fastened with conviction that I lacked things ordinary, even that understanding and wisdom that other Christians had. On this word I mused, and could not tell what to do; especially this word faith pressed me hard, for I could not help it, but at times had to question whether I had any faith or not. For I feared that this lack shut me out of all the blessings that God had given other good people; but I was loath to conclude I had no faith in my soul; for if I do so, I thought, then I shall count myself an utter castaway indeed.

48. No, I said to myself, though I am convinced that I am an ignorant dolt, and that I lack those blessed gifts of knowledge and understanding that other good people have, yet I will venture to conclude that I am not altogether faithless, though I do not know what faith is. For it was shown me, and that too, as I have seen since, by Satan, that those who conclude themselves to be in a faithless state have neither rest nor quiet in their souls; and I was loath to fall quite into despair.

49. So, by this suggestion, I was for a while made afraid to see my lack of faith; but God would not allow me thus to undo and destroy my soul, but continually, against this blind and sad conclusion of mine, created within me such suppositions that I might be deceiving myself in this, that I could not rest content until I came to some certain knowledge whether I had faith or not; this always running in my mind: “But what if you lack faith indeed? But how can you tell you have faith?” And besides, I saw for certain that if I did not have it, I was sure to perish forever.

50. So though I tried at first to pass over the business of faith, yet in a little time, considering the matter better, I was willing to put myself to the trial whether I had faith or not. But alas, poor wretch, so ignorant and brutish was I that at that time I knew no more how to do it than I know how to begin and accomplish that rare and intricate piece of art which I never yet saw or considered.

51. So, while I was thus considering, and being put to my wits’ end about it (for you must know that as yet I had opened my mind in this matter to no man, but only heard and considered), the tempter came in with his delusion: that there was no way for me to know I had faith but by trying to work some miracle; urging those Scriptures that seem to look that way, to enforce and strengthen his temptation. Indeed, one day as I was between Elstow and Bedford, the temptation was hot upon me to try if I had faith by doing some miracle; and the miracle at that time was this: I must say to the puddles that were in the horse tracks, “Be dry,” and to the dry places, “Be puddles.” And truly, at one time I was going to say so indeed; but just as I was about to speak, this thought came into my mind: “But go under that hedge over there and pray first, that God would make you able.” But when I had decided to pray, this came hot upon me: that if I prayed, and came again and tried to do it, and yet did nothing for all that, then be sure I had no faith, but was a castaway and lost. No, I thought, if it is so, I will not try yet, but will wait a little longer.

52. So I continued at a great loss; for I thought, if only those had faith who could do such wonderful things, then I concluded that for the present I neither had it, nor was ever likely to have it in time to come. Thus I was tossed between the devil and my own ignorance, and so perplexed, especially at times, that I could not tell what to do.

53. About this time, the state and happiness of these poor people at Bedford was presented to me in this way, in a kind of vision. I saw them as if they were set on the sunny side of some high mountain, there refreshing themselves with the pleasant beams of the sun, while I was shivering and shrinking in the cold, afflicted with frost, snow, and dark clouds. I thought, also, that between me and them I saw a wall that encircled this mountain; now, through this wall my soul greatly desired to pass, concluding that if I could, I would go even into the very midst of them, and there also comfort myself with the heat of their sun.

54. I thought I went about this wall again and again, continually prying as I went, to see if I could find some way or passage by which I might enter in; but for some time I could find none. At last I saw, as it were, a narrow gap, like a little doorway in the wall, through which I attempted to pass. Now, the passage being very strait and narrow, I made many attempts to get in, but all in vain, until I was almost quite worn out by striving to get in. At last, with great striving, I thought I first got in my head, and after that, by a sidling striving, my shoulders, and my whole body; then I was exceedingly glad, and went and sat down in the midst of them, and so was comforted with the light and heat of their sun.

55. Now, this mountain and wall, etc., was made out to me in this way: the mountain signified the church of the living God; the sun that shone on it, the comforting shining of His merciful face on those who were in it; the wall, I thought, was the Word, which made a separation between the Christians and the world; and the gap in this wall, I thought, was Jesus Christ, who is the way to God the Father (John 14:6; Matt 7:14). But since the passage was wonderfully narrow, so narrow that I could not enter in except with great difficulty, it showed me that none could enter into life but those who were in downright earnest, and unless they also left this wicked world behind them; for here there was room only for body and soul, but not for body and soul and sin.

56. This figure stayed on my spirit many days. All that time I saw myself in a forlorn and sad condition, but yet I was stirred to a vehement hunger and desire to be one of that number who sat in the sunshine. Now also I would pray wherever I was, whether at home or away, in house or field, and would also often, with lifting up of heart, sing that line of the 51st Psalm, “O Lord, consider my distress”; for as yet I did not know where I was.

57. Nor as yet could I attain to any comforting persuasion that I had faith in Christ; but instead of having satisfaction, I now began to find my soul assaulted with fresh doubts about my future happiness, especially with such as these: “Am I elected? But what if the day of grace should now be past and gone?”

58. By these two temptations I was very much afflicted and disquieted, sometimes by one, and sometimes by the other of them. And first, to speak of my questioning my election: I found at this time that though I was in a flame to find the way to heaven and glory, and though nothing could beat me off from this, yet this question so troubled and discouraged me that I was, especially at some times, as if the very strength of my body had also been taken away by its force and power. This scripture also seemed to me to trample on all my desires: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom 9:16).

59. With this scripture I could not tell what to do; for I clearly saw that unless the great God, of His infinite grace and bounty, had voluntarily chosen me to be a vessel of mercy, though I should desire, and long, and labor until my heart broke, no good could come of it. Therefore this question would always stick with me: “How can you tell you are elected? And what if you are not? What then?”

60. “O Lord,” I thought, “what if I am not, indeed?” “It may be you are not,” said the tempter. “It may be so, indeed,” I thought. “Why, then,” said Satan, “you might as well leave off, and strive no further; for if indeed you should not be elected and chosen by God, there is no talk of your being saved; ‘for it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.’”

61. By these things I was driven to my wits’ end, not knowing what to say, or how to answer these temptations. Indeed, I little thought that it was Satan who had assaulted me in this way; I thought rather that it was my own prudence to raise the question. That only the elect attained eternal life I heartily embraced without scruple; but whether I myself was one of them, there lay the question.

62. So for several days I was greatly assaulted and perplexed, and often, when I was walking, I was ready to sink where I went, with faintness in my mind. But one day, after I had been oppressed and cast down by it for so many weeks, as I was now quite giving up the ghost of all my hopes of ever attaining life, that sentence fell with weight upon my spirit: “Look at the generations of old, and see: has anyone ever trusted in God and been confounded?”

63. At this I was greatly lightened and encouraged in my soul; for at that very instant it was expounded to me in this way: “Begin at the beginning of Genesis, and read to the end of the Revelation, and see if you can find that there was anyone who ever trusted in the Lord and was confounded.” So, coming home, I went at once to my Bible to see if I could find that saying, not doubting that I would find it at once; for it was so fresh, and with such strength and comfort on my spirit, that it was as if it talked with me.

64. Well, I looked, but I did not find it; only it stayed with me. Then I asked first this good man, and then another, if they knew where it was, but they knew of no such place. At this I wondered that such a sentence should so suddenly, and with such comfort and strength, seize and stay upon my heart, and yet that no one could find it; for I did not doubt that it was in Holy Scripture.

65. So I continued above a year, and could not find the place; but at last, casting my eye into the books of the Apocrypha, I found it in Ecclesiasticus 2:10. At first this somewhat daunted me; but because by this time I had gained more experience of the love and kindness of God, it troubled me the less, especially when I considered that though it was not in those texts that we call holy and canonical, yet since this sentence was the sum and substance of many of the promises, it was my duty to take the comfort of it. And I bless God for that word, for it was of God to me: that word still, at times, shines before my face.

66. After this, that other doubt came with strength upon me: “But what if the day of grace should be past and gone? What if you have overstayed the time of mercy?” Now, I remember that one day, as I was walking into the country, I was much in the thoughts of this: “But what if the day of grace is past?” And to aggravate my trouble, the tempter presented to my mind those good people of Bedford, and suggested this to me: that these, being converted already, were all that God would save in those parts; and that I came too late, for these had gotten the blessing before I came.

67. Now I was in great distress, thinking in very deed that this might well be so. So I went up and down bemoaning my sad condition, counting myself far worse than a thousand fools for standing off so long, and spending so many years in sin as I had done, continually crying out, “Oh, that I had turned sooner! Oh, that I had turned seven years ago!” It also made me angry with myself to think that I should have had no more sense than to trifle away my time until my soul and heaven were lost.

68. But when I had been long vexed with this fear, and was scarcely able to take one step more, just about the same place where I received my other encouragement, these words broke in upon my mind: “Compel them to come in, so that my house will be full”; “and still there is room” (Luke 14:22, 23). These words, but especially these, “And still there is room,” were sweet words to me; for truly I thought that by them I saw that there was place enough in heaven for me; and moreover, that when the Lord Jesus spoke these words, He was then thinking of me; and that He, knowing that the time would come when I would be afflicted with fear that there was no place left for me in His bosom, spoke this word beforehand and left it on record, so that I might find help by it against this vile temptation. This I then truly believed.

69. In the light and encouragement of this word I went on for a good while; and the comfort was all the greater when I thought that the Lord Jesus should think of me so long ago, and that He should speak those words on purpose for my sake; for I truly thought that He spoke them on purpose to encourage me with them.

70. But I was not without my temptations to go back again: temptations, I say, from Satan, from my own heart, and from carnal acquaintances. But I thank God these were outweighed by that sound sense of death and of the day of judgment, which stayed, as it were, continually in my view. I would also often think of Nebuchadnezzar, of whom it is said, “He had given him all the kingdoms of the earth” (Dan 5:19). “Yet,” I thought, “if this great man had all his portion in this world, one hour in hell fire would make him forget it all.” This consideration was a great help to me.

71. About this time I was also made to see something concerning the beasts that Moses counted clean and unclean. I thought those beasts were types of men: the clean, types of those who were the people of God; but the unclean, types of such as were the children of the wicked one. Now, I read that the clean beasts “chewed the cud”; that is, I thought, they show us that we must feed upon the Word of God. They also parted “the hoof”; I thought that signified that we must part with the ways of ungodly men, if we would be saved. And also, in reading further about them, I found that though we chewed the cud as the hare does, yet if we walked with claws like a dog, or if we parted the hoof like the swine, yet if we did not chew the cud as the sheep does, we were still, for all that, only unclean. For I thought the hare to be a type of those who talk of the Word, yet walk in ways of sin; and that the swine was like him who parts with his outward pollutions, but still lacks the Word of faith, without which there could be no way of salvation, however devout a man may be (Deut 14). After this I found, by reading the Word, that those who must be glorified with Christ in another world must be called by Him here: called to share in His Word and righteousness, and in the comforts and firstfruits of His Spirit, and to a special share in all those heavenly things which indeed fit the soul beforehand for that rest and house of glory which is in heaven above.

72. Here again I was at a very great stand, not knowing what to do, fearing I was not called; for, I thought, if I am not called, what then can do me good? None but those who are effectually called inherit the kingdom of heaven. But oh, how I now loved those words that spoke of a Christian’s calling, as when the Lord said to one, “Follow Me,” and to another, “Come after Me.” And oh, I thought, if only He would say so to me too, how gladly I would run after Him!

73. I cannot now express with what longings and breathings in my soul I cried to Christ to call me. I continued like this for a time, all on a flame to be converted to Jesus Christ; and I also saw at that day such glory in a converted state that I could not be content without a share in it. Gold! If it could have been gotten for gold, what would I not have given for it! Had I had a whole world, it would all have gone ten thousand times over for this, that my soul might have been in a converted state.

74. How lovely now was everyone in my eyes whom I thought to be converted men and women! They shone, they walked like a people who carried the broad seal of heaven about them. Oh, I saw the lot had fallen to them in pleasant places, and they had a goodly heritage (Ps 16:6). But what made me sick at heart was that saying of Christ in Mark: “He went up on the mountain and called for those He willed, and they came to Him” (Mark 3:13).

75. This scripture made me faint and fear, yet it kindled fire in my soul. What made me fear was this: that Christ might have no liking for me, for He called “those He willed.” But oh, the glory that I saw in that condition continually so engaged my heart that I could seldom read of anyone whom Christ called but I at once wished, “I wish I had been in their clothes! I wish I had been born Peter! I wish I had been born John!” or, “I wish I had been standing by and had heard Him when He called them: how I would have cried, ‘O Lord, call me also!’” But oh, I feared He would not call me.

76. And truly the Lord let me go on like this for many months together, and showed me nothing, either that I was already called, or that I would be called hereafter. But at last, after much time spent, and many groans to God that I might be made a partaker of the holy and heavenly calling, that word came in upon me: “I will cleanse their blood, which I have not cleansed, for the Lord dwells in Zion” (Joel 3:21). These words, I thought, were sent to encourage me to keep waiting upon God, and signified to me that if I was not already truly converted to Christ, yet the time might come when I would be.

77. About this time I began to open my mind to those poor people in Bedford, and to tell them my condition. When they had heard it, they told Mr. Gifford about me, and he himself also took occasion to talk with me, and was willing to think well of me, though I think on but little grounds. He invited me to his house, where I would hear him talk with others about the dealings of God with their souls; from all of which I received more and more conviction, and from that time began to see something of the emptiness and inward wretchedness of my wicked heart, for as yet I knew no great matter of it. But now it began to be revealed to me, and also to work to a degree it never had before. Now I clearly found that lusts and corruptions put themselves forth within me, in wicked thoughts and desires, which I had not noticed before; my desires for heaven and life also began to fail. I found also that whereas before my soul was full of longings after God, now it began to hanker after every foolish vanity. Indeed, my heart would not be moved to attend to what was good; it began to be careless both of my soul and of heaven; it would now continually hang back, both from going to every duty and in it; and it was like a clog on the leg of a bird, to hinder me from flying.

78. “No,” I thought, “now I grow worse and worse; now I am farther from conversion than I ever was before.” So I began to sink greatly in my soul, and began to entertain such discouragement in my heart as laid me as low as hell. If I were now to have been burned at the stake, I could not believe that Christ had love for me. Alas, I could neither hear Him, nor see Him, nor feel Him, nor savor any of His things. I was driven as with a tempest; my heart would be unclean; the Canaanites would dwell in the land.

79. Sometimes I would tell my condition to the people of God, and when they heard it, they would pity me, and would tell me of the promises. But they might as well have told me that I must reach the sun with my finger as have bidden me receive or rely on the promise; and as soon as I tried to do it, all my sense and feeling were against me, and I saw I had a heart that would sin, and that lay under a law that would condemn.

80. These things have often made me think of the child whom the father brought to Christ, who, while he was still coming to Him, was thrown down by the devil, and also so rent and torn by him that he lay and wallowed, foaming (Luke 9:42; Mark 9:20).

81. Further, in these days I would find my heart shut itself up against the Lord and against His holy Word. I have found my unbelief set, as it were, its shoulder to the door to keep Him out, and that even when I have cried with many a bitter sigh, “Good Lord, break it open! Lord, break these gates of bronze, and cut through the bars of iron!” (Ps 107:16). Yet that word would sometimes create a peaceful pause in my heart: “I girded you, though you have not known Me” (Isa 45:5).

82. But all this while, as to the act of sinning, I was never more tender than now. My hinder parts were inward; I dared not take a pin or a stick, even one no bigger than a straw, for my conscience was now sore, and would smart at every touch. I could not now tell how to speak my words, for fear I should misplace them. Oh, how gingerly I then went in all I did or said! I found myself as on a miry bog that shook if I did but stir, and felt as if I were left there by God and Christ and the Spirit and all good things.

83. But I observe that though I was such a great sinner before conversion, God never much charged the guilt of the sins of my ignorance upon me; He only showed me that I was lost if I did not have Christ, because I had been a sinner. I saw that I lacked a perfect righteousness to present me without fault before God, and that this righteousness was nowhere to be found but in the person of Jesus Christ.

84. But my original and inward pollution, that, that was my plague and my affliction; that I saw, at a dreadful rate, always putting itself forth within me; whose guilt I felt to an astonishing degree; because of that I was more loathsome in my own eyes than a toad, and I thought I was so in God’s eyes too. Sin and corruption, I said, would bubble out of my heart as naturally as water bubbles out of a fountain. I thought now that everyone had a better heart than I had; I could have exchanged hearts with anybody; I thought none but the devil himself could equal me for inward wickedness and pollution of mind. So at the sight of my own vileness I fell deeply into despair; for I concluded that this condition I was in could not stand with a state of grace. “Surely,” I thought, “I am forsaken by God; surely I am given up to the devil, and to a reprobate mind.” And so I continued a long while, even for some years together.

85. While I was so afflicted with the fears of my own damnation, there were two things that would make me wonder. The one was when I saw old people hunting after the things of this life, as if they would live here always; the other was when I found professing Christians much distressed and cast down when they met with outward losses, as of husband, wife, child, etc. “Lord,” I thought, “what a fuss is made here about such little things as these! What seeking after carnal things by some, and what grief in others for the loss of them! If they labor so much after the things of this present life, and spend so many tears for them, how am I to be bemoaned, pitied, and prayed for! My soul is dying, my soul is damning. If only my soul were in a good condition, and if only I were sure of it, ah, how rich I would count myself, though blessed with nothing but bread and water! I would count those things only small afflictions, and would bear them as little burdens. ‘But a wounded spirit, who can bear?’”

86. And though I was so troubled, and tossed, and afflicted with the sight and sense and terror of my own wickedness, yet I was afraid to let this sense and sight go quite off my mind; for I found that unless guilt of conscience was taken off the right way, that is, by the blood of Christ, a man grew rather worse for the loss of his trouble of mind than better. So if my guilt lay hard upon me, then I would cry that the blood of Christ might take it off; and if it was going off without it (for the sense of sin would sometimes be as if it would die and go quite away), then I would also strive to fetch it back upon my heart again, by bringing the punishment for sin in hell fire upon my spirit; and I would cry, “Lord, do not let it go off my heart except the right way, by the blood of Christ, and by the application of Your mercy, through Him, to my soul.” For that scripture lay heavily upon me: “Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Heb 9:22). And what made me the more afraid of this was that I had seen some who, when they were under wounds of conscience, would cry and pray; yet, seeking present ease from their trouble rather than pardon for their sin, they did not care how they lost their guilt, so long as they got it out of their mind. Now, having got it off the wrong way, it was not sanctified to them; but they grew harder and blinder, and more wicked after their trouble. This made me afraid, and made me cry to God the more that it might not be so with me.

87. And now I was sorry that God had made me a man, for I feared I was a reprobate. I counted man, as unconverted, the most miserable of all the creatures. Being so afflicted and tossed about my sad condition, I counted myself alone, and more unblessed than most men.

88. Indeed, I thought it impossible that I should ever attain to so much goodness of heart as to thank God that He had made me a man. Man indeed is the most noble of all creatures in the visible world by creation; but by sin he had made himself the most ignoble. The beasts, birds, fishes, etc.: I counted their condition blessed, for they did not have a sinful nature; they were not liable to the wrath of God; they were not to go to hell fire after death. So I could have rejoiced had my condition been as any of theirs.

89. In this condition I went on a great while; but when comforting time had come, I heard one preach a sermon on these words in Song 4:1: “How beautiful you are, my love—how very beautiful!” But at that time he made these two words, “My love,” his chief subject matter; from which, after he had opened the text a little, he drew these several conclusions: 1. That the church, and so every saved soul, is Christ’s love, when loveless. 2. Christ’s love without a cause. 3. Christ’s love when hated by the world. 4. Christ’s love when under temptation, and under desertion. 5. Christ’s love from first to last.

90. But I gained nothing from what he said at the time, except that when he came to the application of the fourth particular, this was the word he said: “If it is so, that the saved soul is Christ’s love when under temptation and desertion, then, poor tempted soul, when you are assaulted and afflicted with temptations, and the hidings of God’s face, yet always think on these two words, ‘My love.’”

91. So as I was going home, these words came again into my thoughts; and I well remember that as they came in, I said this in my heart: “What shall I get by thinking on these two words?” This thought had no sooner passed through my heart than these words began to kindle in my spirit: “You are my love, you are my dove,” twenty times together. And continually, as they ran this way in my mind, they grew stronger and warmer, and began to make me look up; but being as yet between hope and fear, I kept replying in my heart, “But is it true? But is it true?” At which that sentence fell upon me, that he “did not know that what was done by the angel was true” (Acts 12:9).

92. Then I began to give place to the word, which with power, over and over, made this joyful sound within my soul: “You are my love, you are my love; and nothing shall separate you from my love”; and with that, Rom 8:39 came into my mind. Now my heart was filled full of comfort and hope, and now I could believe that my sins would be forgiven me. Indeed, I was now so taken with the love and mercy of God that I remember I did not know how to contain myself until I got home. I thought I could have spoken of His love, and told of His mercy to me, even to the very crows that sat on the plowed lands before me, had they been able to understand me. So I said in my soul with much gladness, “Well, I wish I had a pen and ink here; I would write this down before I go any further, for surely I will not forget this forty years from now.” But alas, within less than forty days I began to question everything again; and at times I fell back into my old ways again, which made me begin to question everything continually.

93. Yet still, at times, I was helped to believe that it was a true manifestation of grace to my soul, though I had lost much of its life and savor. Now about a week or a fortnight after this, I was much followed by this scripture: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has desired to have you+” (Luke 22:31). And sometimes it would sound so loud within me, and, as it were, call so strongly after me, that once above all the rest I turned my head over my shoulder, truly thinking that some man behind me had called me, though he was at a great distance; he called so loud, I thought. It came, as I have thought since, to stir me up to prayer and to watchfulness; it came to let me know that a cloud and a storm were coming down upon me; but I did not understand it.

94. Also, as I remember, that time that it called to me so loud was the last time that it sounded in my ears; but I think I still hear with what a loud voice these words, “Simon, Simon,” sounded in my ears. I truly thought, as I have told you, that somebody half a mile behind me had called after me; and although that was not my name, yet it made me suddenly look behind me, believing that he who called so loud meant me.

95. But I was so foolish and ignorant that I did not know the reason for this sound, which, as I both saw and felt soon after, was sent from heaven as an alarm, to awaken me to provide for what was coming. Only I would muse and wonder in my mind, to think what could be the reason that this scripture, and that at this rate, so often and so loud, should continually be sounding and rattling in my ears. But, as I said before, I soon after perceived God’s purpose in it.

96. For about the space of a month after, a very great storm came down upon me, which handled me twenty times worse than all I had met with before. It came stealing upon me, now by one piece, then by another. First, all my comfort was taken from me; then darkness seized upon me; after which whole floods of blasphemies, against God, Christ, and the Scriptures, were poured upon my spirit, to my great confusion and astonishment. These blasphemous thoughts were such as stirred up questions in me against the very being of God, and of His only beloved Son: whether there were, in truth, a God, or a Christ? And whether the holy Scriptures were not rather a fable and a cunning story than the holy and pure Word of God?

97. The tempter would also assault me much with this: “How can you tell but that the Turks had as good Scriptures to prove their Muhammad the Savior as we have to prove our Jesus is? And could I think that so many ten thousands, in so many countries and kingdoms, should be without the knowledge of the right way to heaven (if there were indeed a heaven), and that we only, who live in a corner of the earth, should alone be blessed with it? Everyone thinks his own religion the rightest, both Jews and Moors and pagans! And what if all our faith, and Christ, and Scriptures, should be only a think-so too?”

98. Sometimes I have tried to argue against these suggestions, and to set some of the sentences of blessed Paul against them; but alas, when I did so, I quickly felt such arguings as these return upon me: “Though we make so great a matter of Paul and of his words, yet how could I tell but that in very deed he, being a subtle and cunning man, might give himself up to deceiving with strong delusions, and also take the pains and labor to undo and destroy his fellows?”

99. These suggestions, with many others which at this time I must not and dare not utter, either by word or by pen, made such a seizure upon my spirit, and so overweighed my heart, with their number, their continuance, and their fiery force, that I felt as if there were nothing else but these within me from morning to night, and as though indeed there could be room for nothing else. I also concluded that God had, in very wrath to my soul, given me up to them, to be carried away with them as with a mighty whirlwind.

100. Only by the distaste that they gave to my spirit, I felt there was something in me that refused to embrace them. But this consideration I had only when God gave me leave to swallow my spittle; otherwise the noise, and strength, and force of these temptations would drown and overflow, and as it were bury, all such thoughts, or the remembrance of any such thing. While I was in this temptation, I would often find my mind suddenly driven to curse and swear, or to speak some grievous thing against God, or Christ His Son, and against the Scriptures.

101. Now I thought, “Surely I am possessed by the devil”; at other times again, I thought I would be bereft of my wits. For instead of praising and magnifying God the Lord with others, if I but heard Him spoken of, at once some most horrible blasphemous thought or other would bolt out of my heart against Him; so that whether I thought that God was, or again thought there was no such thing, I could feel no love, nor peace, nor gracious disposition within me.

102. These things sank me into very deep despair; for I concluded that such things could not possibly be found among those who loved God. When these temptations were upon me with force, I often compared myself to the case of a child whom some gypsy has taken up by force in her arms, and is carrying away from friends and country. Kick I sometimes did, and also shriek and cry; but yet I was as if bound in the wings of the temptation, and the wind would carry me away. I thought also of Saul, and of the evil spirit that possessed him, and greatly feared that my condition was the same as his (1 Sam 16:14).

103. In these days, when I heard others talk of what the sin against the Holy Spirit was, then the tempter would so provoke me to desire to sin that sin that I was as if I could not, must not, and should not be quiet until I had committed it. Now no sin would serve but that. If it were to be committed by speaking such a word, then I have been as if my mouth would have spoken that word, whether I wanted to or not; and so strongly was this temptation upon me that often I have been ready to clap my hand under my chin, to hold my mouth from opening; and to that end I have also had thoughts at other times of leaping headfirst into some dunghill hole or other, to keep my mouth from speaking.

104. Now again I looked at the condition of the dog and the toad, and counted the state of everything that God had made far better than this dreadful state of mine, and than such as my companions’ was. Indeed, I would gladly have been in the condition of a dog or a horse, for I knew they had no soul to perish under the everlasting weight of hell, or of sin, as mine was likely to do. No, and though I saw this, felt this, and was broken to pieces with it, yet what added to my sorrow was that I could not find that I desired deliverance with all my soul. That scripture also tore and rent my soul in the midst of this turmoil: “The wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck. ‘There is no peace,’ says my God, ‘for the wicked.’”

105. And now my heart was at times exceedingly hard. If I would have given a thousand pounds for a tear, I could not shed one; no, nor sometimes scarcely desire to shed one. I was much dejected to think that this would be my lot. I saw some could mourn and lament their sin; and others, again, could rejoice and bless God for Christ; and others, again, could quietly talk of the Word of God, and remember it with gladness; while I alone was in the storm or tempest. This sank me much; I thought my condition was alone. So I would much bewail my hard lot; but get out of these things, or get rid of them, I could not.

106. While this temptation lasted, which was about a year, I could attend none of the ordinances of God but with sore and great affliction. Indeed, I was then most distressed with blasphemies. If I was hearing the Word, then uncleanness, blasphemies, and despair would hold me captive there; if I was reading, then sometimes I had sudden thoughts to question all I read; sometimes, again, my mind would be so strangely snatched away, and possessed with other things, that I neither knew, nor regarded, nor remembered so much as the sentence that I had just now read.

107. In prayer also I was greatly troubled at this time. Sometimes I thought I would see the devil; indeed, I thought I felt him behind me, pulling my clothes. He would also be continually at me in time of prayer to stop: “Break off, make haste, you have prayed enough, and stay no longer,” continually drawing my mind away. Sometimes also he would cast in such wicked thoughts as these: that I must pray to him, or for him. I have sometimes thought of that: “Fall down,” or, “if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt 4:9).

108. Also, when, because I had wandering thoughts in the time of this duty, I have labored to compose my mind and fix it upon God, then with great force the tempter has labored to distract me and confound me, and to turn away my mind, by presenting to my heart and imagination the form of a bush, a bull, a broom, or the like, as if I should pray to those. To these also he would, at some times especially, so hold my mind that I was as if I could think of nothing else, or pray to nothing else, but these, or such as they.

109. Yet at times I would have some strong and heart-affecting perceptions of God, and of the reality of the truth of His gospel; but oh, how my heart would at such times put itself forth with inexpressible groanings! My whole soul was then in every word; I would cry with pangs after God that He would be merciful to me. But then I would be daunted again with such fancies as these: I would think that God mocked at these prayers of mine, saying, and that in the hearing of the holy angels, “This poor simple wretch hankers after Me as if I had nothing to do with My mercy but to bestow it on such as he. Alas, poor soul! How you are deceived! It is not for such as you to have favor with the Highest.”

110. Then the tempter has also come upon me with such discouragements as these: “You are very hot for mercy, but I will cool you; this frame will not last always; many have been as hot as you for a spurt, but I have quenched their zeal.” And with this, such and such who had fallen away would be set before my eyes. Then I would be afraid that I would do so too; but, I thought, “I am glad this comes into my mind. Well, I will watch, and take what heed I can.” “Though you do,” said Satan, “I shall be too hard for you; I will cool you imperceptibly, by degrees, little by little. What do I care,” he says, “though I am seven years chilling your heart, if I can do it at last? Continual rocking will lull a crying child to sleep. I will ply it close, but I will have my end accomplished. Though you are burning hot at present, yet if I can pull you from this fire, I shall have you cold before long.”

111. These things brought me into great straits; for as I could not at present find myself fit for present death, so I thought that to live long would make me yet more unfit; for time would make me forget everything, and wear even the remembrance of the evil of sin, the worth of heaven, and the need I had of the blood of Christ to wash me, out of both mind and thought. But I thank Christ Jesus these things did not at present make me slack in my crying, but rather put me more upon it, like the woman who met with the adulterer (Deut 22:27). In those days that was a good word to me, after I had suffered these things a while: “I am convinced that neither height nor depth, nor death nor life,” etc., “will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 8:38). And now I hoped long life would not destroy me, nor make me miss heaven.

112. Yet I had some supports in this temptation, though they were then all questioned by me. That in the third of Jeremiah, at the first, was something to me, and so was the consideration of the fifth verse of that chapter: that though we have spoken and done as evil things as we could, yet we should cry to God, “My Father, You are my friend from youth,” and should return to Him.

113. I had, also, once a sweet glance from that in 2 Corinthians 5:21: “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” I remember that one day, as I was sitting in a neighbor’s house, very sad there at the consideration of my many blasphemies, and as I was saying in my mind, “What ground do I have to think that I, who have been so vile and abominable, should ever inherit eternal life?” that word came suddenly upon me: “What then shall we say in response to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom 8:31). That also was a help to me: “Because I live, you+ also will live” (John 14:19). But these words were only hints, touches, and short visits, though very sweet when present; only they did not last, but, like Peter’s sheet, they were suddenly caught up from me to heaven again (Acts 10:16).

114. But afterward the Lord revealed Himself to me more fully and graciously; and indeed He completely delivered me, not only from the guilt that these things had laid upon my conscience, but also from their very filth; for the temptation was removed, and I was put into my right mind again, as other Christians were.

115. I remember that one day, as I was traveling into the country and musing on the wickedness and blasphemy of my heart, and considering the enmity that was in me against God, that scripture came into my mind: He has “made peace through the blood of His cross” (Col 1:20). By this I was made to see, again and again that day, that God and my soul were friends by this blood; yes, I saw that the justice of God and my sinful soul could embrace and kiss each other through this blood. This was a good day to me; I hope I shall not forget it.

116. At another time, as I sat by the fire in my house, musing on my wretchedness, the Lord made this also a precious word to me: “Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death” (Heb 2:14, 15). I thought that the glory of those words was then so weighty on me that I was, once and twice, ready to faint as I sat; yet not with grief and trouble, but with solid joy and peace.

117. At this time, also, I sat under the ministry of holy Mr. Gifford, whose doctrine, by God’s grace, did much for my stability. This man made it much his business to deliver the people of God from all those false and unsound rests that by nature we are prone to take and make for our souls. He would bid us take special care that we did not take up any truth on trust, as from this or that or any other man or men, but cry mightily to God that He would convince us of the reality of it, and settle us in it by His own Spirit in the holy Word. “For,” he said, “if you+ do otherwise, when temptations come, if they come strongly, you+, not having received these truths with evidence from heaven, will find that you+ lack the help and strength to resist that you+ once thought you+ had.”

118. This was as timely to my soul as the former and latter rain in their season; for I had found, and that by sad experience, the truth of these words of his. For I had felt that “no man can say,” especially when tempted by the devil, “that Jesus Christ is Lord except by the Holy Spirit.” So I found my soul, through grace, very ready to drink in this doctrine, and inclined to pray to God that, in nothing that concerned God’s glory and my own eternal happiness, He would allow me to be without its confirmation from heaven. For now I saw clearly that there was an exceedingly great difference between the notions of flesh and blood and the revelations of God in heaven; and also a great difference between the faith that is feigned, and according to man’s wisdom, and the faith that comes by a man’s being born to it of God (Matt 16:15–17; 1 John 5:1).

119. But oh, how my soul was now led from truth to truth by God! even from the birth and cradle of the Son of God to His ascension and His second coming from heaven to judge the world.

120. Truly, I then found, on this account, that the great God was very good to me; for, as far as I remember, there was not anything that I then cried to God to make known and reveal to me but He was pleased to do it for me; I mean that there was not one part of the gospel of the Lord Jesus but I was led into it in order. It seemed to me that I saw with great evidence, from the account of the four evangelists, the wonderful work of God in giving Jesus Christ to save us, from His conception and birth even to His second coming to judgment. It was as if I had seen Him born, as if I had seen Him grow up, as if I had seen Him walk through this world, from the cradle to the cross: and when He came to the cross, I saw how gently He gave Himself to be hanged and nailed on it for my sins and wicked doings. Also, as I was musing on this progress of His, this dropped on my spirit: “He was ordained for the slaughter” (1 Pet 1:19, 20).

121. When I have also considered the truth of His resurrection, and have remembered that word, “Do not touch Me, Mary,” and so on, I have seen as if He had leaped out of the grave’s mouth for joy that He was risen again, and had gotten the victory over our dreadful foes (John 20:17). I have also, in the spirit, seen Him a man at the right hand of God the Father for me, and have seen the manner of His coming from heaven to judge the world with glory, and have been confirmed in these things by these scriptures following: Acts 1:9, 10; 7:56; 10:42; Heb 7:24; 8:3; Rev 1:18; 1 Thess 4:17, 18.

122.
