Once I was troubled to know whether the Lord Jesus was man as well as God, and God as well as man; and truly, in those days, let men say what they would, unless I had it with evidence from heaven, it was all nothing to me; I did not count myself settled in any truth of God. Well, I was much troubled about this point, and could not tell how to be satisfied. At last that verse in the fifth chapter of Revelation came into my mind: “And I looked, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb.” In the midst of the throne, I thought, there is His Godhead; in the midst of the elders, there is His manhood. Oh, how this seemed to me to glitter! It was a goodly touch, and gave me sweet satisfaction. That other scripture also helped me much in this: “Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace,” and so on (Isa 9:6).

123. Also, besides these teachings of God in His Word, the Lord made use of two things to confirm me in this truth: the one was the errors of the Quakers, and the other was the guilt of sin. For as the Quakers opposed this truth, so God confirmed me in it all the more, by leading me into the scriptures that wonderfully maintain it.

124. The errors that this people then maintained were:

1. That the holy Scriptures were not the Word of God.

2. That every man in the world had the spirit of Christ, grace, faith, and so on.

3. That Christ Jesus, as crucified, and dying sixteen hundred years ago, did not satisfy divine justice for the sins of His people.

4. That Christ’s flesh and blood was within the saints.

5. That the bodies of the good and bad that are buried in the churchyard shall not rise again.

6. That the resurrection is already past with good men.

7. That the man Jesus, who was crucified between two thieves on Mount Calvary, in the land of Canaan, near Jerusalem, had not ascended up above the starry heavens.

8. That He, the very same Jesus who died by the hand of the Jews, would not come again at the last day, and as man judge all nations, and so on.

125. Many more vile and abominable things were stirred up by them in those days, by which I was driven to a closer search of the Scripture, and was, through its light and testimony, not only enlightened but greatly confirmed and comforted in the truth. And, as I said, the guilt of sin helped me much; for whenever that came upon me, the blood of Christ took it off again, and again, and again, and that sweetly too, according to the Scriptures. O friends, cry to God to reveal Jesus Christ to you+; there is none who teaches like Him.

126. It would take too long to stay here and tell you in detail how God settled me in all the things of Christ, and how, so that He might do so, He led me into His words; yes, and also how He opened them to me, and made them shine before me, and caused them to dwell with me, talk with me, and comfort me over and over, concerning both His own being and the being of His Son, and Spirit, and Word, and gospel.

127. Only this, as I said before, I will say to you again: in general He was pleased to take this course with me. First He allowed me to be afflicted with temptation concerning these things, and then He revealed them to me. For example, at times I would lie under great guilt for sin, even crushed to the ground with it, and then the Lord would show me the death of Christ; yes, and so sprinkle my conscience with His blood that I would find, and that before I was aware, that in the very conscience where just now the law reigned and raged, there the peace and love of God through Christ would rest and abide.

128. Now I had an evidence, as I thought, of my salvation from heaven, with many golden seals on it, all hanging in my sight. Now I could remember this manifestation and that other revelation of grace with comfort, and would often long and desire that the last day had come, that I might be forever inflamed with the sight and joy and communion of Him whose head was crowned with thorns, whose face was spit on, and body broken, and soul made an offering for my sins. For whereas before I lay continually trembling at the mouth of hell, now it seemed to me I had got so far from it that, when I looked back, I could scarcely make it out. And oh, I thought, if only I were eighty years old now, that I might die quickly, that my soul might be gone to rest.

129. But before I had got this far out of these temptations of mine, I greatly longed to see the experience of some ancient godly man who had written some hundreds of years before I was born. For as for those who had written in our days, I thought (but I ask them now to pardon me) that they had written only what others felt, or else had, through the strength of their wits and abilities, studied to answer such objections as they saw others were perplexed with, without going down into the deep themselves. Well, after many such longings in my mind, the God in whose hand are all our days and ways cast into my hand one day a book of Martin Luther’s; it was his commentary on Galatians, and it was so old that it was ready to fall apart piece by piece if I did but turn it over. Now I was much pleased that such an old book had fallen into my hand; and when I had read only a little way in it, I found my condition so fully and profoundly handled in his experience that it was as if his book had been written out of my heart. This made me marvel; for this is what I thought: “This man could not know anything of the state of Christians now, but must surely write and speak the experience of former days.”

130. Besides, in that book he also debates most gravely the rise of these temptations, namely, blasphemy, despair, and the like, showing that the law of Moses, as well as the devil, death, and hell, has a very great hand in them. At first this was very strange to me; but by considering and watching, I found it so indeed. But I intend nothing of particulars here; only this, I think, I must declare before all men: I prefer this book of Martin Luther upon Galatians, except the Holy Bible, before all the books that I have ever seen, as most fit for a wounded conscience.

131. And now I found, as I thought, that I loved Christ dearly. Oh, it seemed to me that my soul clung to Him, my affections clung to Him; I felt love to Him as hot as fire. And now, as Job said, I thought I should die in my nest. But I quickly found that my great love was only little, and that I, who had, as I thought, such burning love to Jesus Christ, could let Him go again for a very trifle. God knows how to humble us, and can hide pride from man. Soon after this my love was tried in earnest.

132. For after the Lord had in this manner so graciously delivered me from this great and severe temptation, and had settled me so sweetly in the faith of His holy gospel, and had given me such strong consolation and blessed evidence from heaven concerning my share in His love through Christ, the tempter came upon me again, and that with a more grievous and dreadful temptation than before.

133. And that was, to “sell and part with this most blessed Christ, to exchange Him for the things of this life, for anything.” The temptation lay upon me for the space of a year, and followed me so continually that I was not free of it one day in a month; no, at times not for one hour in many days together, unless I was asleep.

134. And though in my judgment I was persuaded that those who were once effectually in Christ (as I hoped, through His grace, I had seen myself to be) could never lose Him forever (“For the land must not be sold forever, for the land is Mine,” says God, Lev 25:23), yet it was a continual vexation to me to think that I should have so much as one such thought within me against a Christ, a Jesus, who had done for me as He had done; and yet at that time I had almost no other thoughts but such blasphemous ones.

135. But neither my dislike of the thought, nor any desire and endeavor to resist it, in the least shook or lessened its continuance, or its force and strength. For it always mixed itself in with almost whatever I thought, in such a way that I could neither eat my food, stoop for a pin, chop a stick, nor cast my eye to look on this or that, but the temptation would always come: “Sell Christ for this, or sell Christ for that; sell Him, sell Him.”

136. Sometimes it would run in my thoughts no fewer than a hundred times together, “Sell Him, sell Him, sell Him.” Against this, I may say, for whole hours together I have been forced to stand as if continually leaning and forcing my spirit against it, lest perhaps, before I was aware, some wicked thought might arise in my heart that might consent to it. And sometimes also the tempter would make me believe I had consented to it, and then I would be as if tortured on a rack for whole days together.

137. This temptation put me in such fright, lest at some time, I say, I should consent to it and be overcome by it, that by the very force of my mind in laboring to contradict and resist this wickedness, my very body would be put into action or motion, by way of pushing or thrusting with my hands or elbows, all the while answering as fast as the destroyer said, “Sell Him”: “I will not, I will not, I will not, I will not; no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands of worlds.” I reckoned so, lest in the midst of these assaults I should set too low a value on Him, even until I scarcely knew where I was, or how to be composed again.

138. At these seasons he would not let me eat my food in quiet; but, of all things, when I was set at the table at my meal, I must go away from it to pray; I must leave my food now, just now, so counterfeit-holy would this devil be too. When I was tempted in this way, I would say within myself, “Now I am at my meal; let me make an end.” “No,” he said, “you must do it now, or you will displease God and despise Christ.” So I was much afflicted with these things; and because of the sinfulness of my nature, imagining that these things were impulses from God, I would refuse to do it, as if I were denying God; and then I would be as guilty, because I did not obey a temptation of the devil, as if I had broken the law of God indeed.

139. But to be brief: one morning, as I lay in my bed, I was, as at other times, most fiercely assaulted with this temptation, to “sell and part with Christ”; the wicked suggestion kept running in my mind, “Sell Him, sell Him, sell Him, sell Him, sell Him,” as fast as a man could speak. Against it also, in my mind, as at other times, I answered, “No, no, not for thousands, thousands, thousands,” at least twenty times together. But at last, after much striving, even until I was almost out of breath, I felt this thought pass through my heart, “Let Him go, if He will!” and I thought also that I felt my heart freely consent to it. Oh, the diligence of Satan! Oh, the desperateness of man’s heart!

140. Now the battle was won, and down I fell, as a bird that is shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt and fearful despair. So, getting out of my bed, I went moping into the field; but God knows, with as heavy a heart as mortal man, I think, could bear. There, for the space of two hours, I was like a man bereft of life, and as now past all recovery, and bound over to eternal punishment.

141. And with that, this scripture seized upon my soul: “Or profane person, like Esau, who for one morsel of food sold his birthright. For you+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears” (Heb 12:16, 17).

142. Now I was as one bound; I felt myself shut up to the judgment to come. For two years together nothing would now abide with me but damnation, and an expectation of damnation; I say, nothing would now abide with me but this, except some few moments of relief, as you will see in what follows.

143. These words were to my soul like fetters of brass on my legs, and I went about in their continual sound for several months together. But about ten or eleven o’clock on that same day, as I was walking under a hedge, full of sorrow and guilt, God knows, and bemoaning myself for this hard lot, that such a thought should arise within me, suddenly this sentence bolted in on me: “The blood of Christ remits all guilt.” At this I made a stand in my spirit; and with that, this word took hold upon me: “The blood of Jesus Christ, His Son, cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

144. Now I began to conceive peace in my soul, and it seemed to me as if I saw the tempter leer and steal away from me, as being ashamed of what he had done. At the same time also I had my sin and the blood of Christ set before me in this way: that my sin, when compared to the blood of Christ, was no more to it than this little clod or stone before me is to this vast and wide field that I see here. This gave me good encouragement for the space of two or three hours; in which time also, it seemed to me, I saw by faith the Son of God suffering for my sins. But because it did not stay, I sank in my spirit under exceedingly great guilt again.

145. But this was chiefly because of the scripture I have mentioned, concerning Esau’s selling of his birthright; for that scripture would lie all day long, all the week long, yes, all the year long in my mind, and hold me down, so that I could by no means lift myself up. For when I would strive to turn to this scripture or that for relief, that sentence would always be sounding in me: “For you+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing—he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.”

146. Sometimes, indeed, I would have a touch from that word in Luke 22:32, “I have prayed for you, that your faith will not fail”; but it would not abide upon me. Nor indeed could I, when I considered my state, find ground to conceive in the least that the root of that grace should be within me, having sinned as I had done. Now I was torn and rent in a heavy case, for many days together.

147. Then I began, with a sad and anxious heart, to consider the nature and largeness of my sin, and to search in the Word of God whether I could find in any place a word of promise, or any encouraging sentence, from which I might take relief. So I began to consider that word in Mark: “The sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter.” This place, it seemed to me at first sight, contained a large and glorious promise for the pardon of great offenses; but considering the place more fully, I thought it was rather to be understood as relating chiefly to those who, while in a natural state, had committed such things as are mentioned there; but not to me, who had not only received light and mercy, but had, both after it and also contrary to it, slighted Christ as I had done.

148. I feared therefore that this wicked sin of mine might be that unpardonable sin of which He speaks there: “But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation” (Mark 3:29). And I gave all the more credit to this because of that sentence in Hebrews: “For you+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” And this stuck with me always.

149. And now I was both a burden and a terror to myself; nor did I ever know so well as now what it was to be weary of my life, and yet afraid to die. Oh, how gladly now would I have been anybody but myself! Anything but a man! and in any condition but my own! For nothing passed more frequently over my mind than that it was impossible for me to be forgiven my transgression, and to be saved from the wrath to come.

150. And now I began to labor to call back the time that was past, wishing a thousand times twice told that the day were yet to come when I should be tempted to such a sin; concluding, with great indignation both against my heart and against all assaults, that I would rather have been torn in pieces than be found consenting to it. But alas! these thoughts and wishings and resolvings were now too late to help me; the thought had passed through my heart; God has let me go, and I have fallen. “Oh,” I thought, “that it were with me as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me!” (Job 29:2).

151. Then again, being loath and unwilling to perish, I began to compare my sin with the sins of others, to see if I could find that any of those who are saved had done as I had done. So I considered David’s adultery and murder, and found them most heinous crimes, and those too committed after light and grace received. But yet, by considering, I perceived that his transgressions were only such as were against the law of Moses, from which the Lord Christ could, with the consent of His Word, deliver him; but mine was against the gospel, yes, against its Mediator; I had sold my Savior.

152. Now again I would be as if racked upon the wheel, when I considered that, besides the guilt that possessed me, I should be so void of grace, so bewitched. What, I thought, must it be no sin but this? Must it necessarily be the “great transgression” (Ps 19:13)? Must that wicked one touch my soul (1 John 5:18)? Oh, what stings I found in all these sentences!

153. What, I thought, is there but one sin that is unpardonable? But one sin that lays the soul beyond the reach of God’s mercy; and must I be guilty of that? Must it necessarily be that one? Is there but one sin among so many millions of sins for which there is no forgiveness; and must I commit this? Oh, unhappy sin! Oh, unhappy man! These things would so break and confound my spirit that I could not tell what to do; I thought at times they would have broken my wits. And always, to aggravate my misery, this would run in my mind: “You+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected.” Oh, no one knows the terrors of those days but myself!

154. After this I came to consider Peter’s sin, which he committed in denying his Master; and indeed, this came nearest to mine of any that I could find. For he had denied his Savior, as I had, after light and mercy received; yes, and that too after warning was given him. I also considered that he did it both once and twice, and that after he had time to consider in between. But though I put all these circumstances together, that if possible I might find help, yet I considered again that his was only a denial of his Master, but mine was a selling of my Savior. So I thought to myself that I came nearer to Judas than to either David or Peter.

155. Here again my torment would flame out and afflict me; yes, it would grind me, as it were, to powder, to consider God’s preservation of others while I fell into the snare. For in thus considering other men’s sins, and comparing them with my own, I could plainly see that God preserved them, notwithstanding their wickedness, and would not let them, as He had let me, become a son of perdition.

156. But oh, how my soul at this time prized the preservation that God set about His people! Ah, how safely I saw them walk, whom God had hedged in! They were within His care, protection, and special providence; though by nature they were fully as bad as I, yet because He loved them, He would not allow them to fall outside the range of mercy. But as for me, I was gone, I had done it; He would not preserve me, nor keep me, but allowed me, because I was a reprobate, to fall as I had done. Now those blessed places that speak of God’s keeping His people shone like the sun before me, though not to comfort me, yet to show me the blessed state and heritage of those whom the Lord had blessed.

157. Now I saw that, as God had His hand in all the providences and dispensations that overtook His elect, so He had His hand in all the temptations that they had to sin against Him; not to incite them to wickedness, but to choose their temptations and troubles for them, and also to leave them for a time to such sins only as might not destroy but humble them, as might not put them beyond, but lay them in the way of, the renewing of His mercy. But oh, what love, what care, what kindness and mercy I now saw mixing itself with the most severe and dreadful of all God’s ways with His people! He would let David, Hezekiah, Solomon, Peter, and others fall, but He would not let them fall into the unpardonable sin, nor into hell for sin. Oh, I thought, these are the men whom God has loved; these are the men whom God, though He chastens them, keeps in safety by Him, and whom He makes to abide under the shadow of the Almighty. But all these thoughts added sorrow, grief, and horror to me, since whatever I now thought on was killing to me. If I thought how God kept His own, that was killing to me. If I thought of how I had fallen myself, that was killing to me. As all things worked together for the best, and to do good to those who were the called according to His purpose, so I thought that all things worked for my harm, and for my eternal overthrow.

158. Then again I began to compare my sin with the sin of Judas, that if possible I might find whether mine differed from that which in truth is unpardonable. And oh, I thought, if it should differ from it, though only by the breadth of a hair, what a happy condition my soul is in! And by considering, I found that Judas did his intentionally, but mine was against my prayer and strivings; besides, his was committed with much deliberation, but mine in a fearful hurry, on a sudden. All this while I was tossed to and fro like the locusts, and driven from trouble to sorrow, always hearing the sound of Esau’s fall in my ears, and of its dreadful consequences.

159. Yet this consideration about Judas and his sin was, for a while, some little relief to me; for I saw that, as to the circumstances, I had not transgressed so foully as he. But this was quickly gone again; for I thought to myself, there might be more ways than one to commit the unpardonable sin; also I thought that there might be degrees of it, as well as of other transgressions. So, for all I could yet perceive, this iniquity of mine might be such as might never be passed by.

160. I was often now ashamed that I should be like such an ugly man as Judas; I thought also how loathsome I would be to all the saints at the day of judgment; so much so that now I could scarcely see a good man, whom I believed to have a good conscience, but I would feel my heart tremble at him while I was in his presence. Oh, now I saw a glory in walking with God, and what a mercy it was to have a good conscience before Him.

161. At about this time I was tempted to content myself by receiving some false opinion, such as that there should be no such thing as a day of judgment, that we should not rise again, and that sin was no such grievous thing. The tempter suggested this: “For even if these things should indeed be true, yet to believe otherwise would give you ease for the present. If you must perish, do not torment yourself so much beforehand; drive the thoughts of damnation out of your mind by filling your mind with some such conclusions as Atheists and Ranters use to help themselves.”

162. But oh, when such thoughts have passed through my heart, how death and judgment have been in my view, as it were within a step! It seemed to me that the Judge stood at the door; it was as if it had come already; so that such things could find no welcome. But I think I see by this that Satan will use any means to keep the soul from Christ. He does not love an awakened frame of spirit; complacency, blindness, darkness, and error are the very kingdom and dwelling place of the wicked one.

163. I found it hard work now to pray to God, because despair was swallowing me up. I thought I was driven away from God as with a tempest; for always when I cried to God for mercy, this would come in: “It is too late; I am lost; God has let me fall, not to my correction, but to condemnation; my sin is unpardonable; and I know concerning Esau how, after he had sold his birthright, he wanted to receive the blessing, but was rejected.” About this time I came upon that dreadful story of that miserable mortal, Francis Spira, a book that was to my troubled spirit as salt rubbed into a fresh wound. Every sentence in that book, every groan of that man, with all the rest of his actions in his anguish, as his tears, his prayers, his gnashing of teeth, his wringing of hands, his twining and twisting, and languishing and pining away under that mighty hand of God that was upon him, was as knives and daggers in my soul. Especially that sentence of his was frightful to me: “Man knows the beginning of sin, but who sets bounds to where it will end?” Then the former sentence, as the conclusion of all, would fall again upon my conscience like a hot thunderbolt: “for you+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.”

164. Then I would be struck into a very great trembling, so much so that at times, for whole days together, I could feel my very body, as well as my mind, shake and totter under the sense of the dreadful judgment of God that should fall on those who have sinned that most fearful and unpardonable sin. I felt also such a clogging and heat at my stomach, because of this terror of mine, that, especially at some times, it was as if my breastbone would have split open. Then I thought of what is said of Judas, who, “falling headlong, burst open in the middle, and all his intestines spilled out” (Acts 1:18).

165. I feared also that this was the mark that the Lord set on Cain, namely, continual fear and trembling under the heavy load of guilt that He had charged on him for the blood of his brother Abel. So I would wind, and twist, and shrink under the burden that was upon me; and this burden so oppressed me that I could neither stand, nor walk, nor lie down, either at rest or quiet.

166. Yet that saying would sometimes come to mind, “He has received gifts for the rebellious” (Ps 68:18). “The rebellious,” I thought; why, surely they are those who were once in subjection to their prince, even those who, after they have sworn subjection to his government, have taken up arms against him. And this, I thought, is my very condition: I once loved Him, feared Him, served Him; but now I am a rebel; I have sold Him; I have said, “Let Him go if He will”; but yet He has gifts for rebels, and then why not for me?

167. I sometimes thought on this, and would labor to take hold of it, so that some refreshment, though small, might be conceived by me; but in this also I missed my desire. I was driven by force beyond it; I was like a man going to the place of execution, even past that place where he would gladly creep in and hide himself, but is not allowed to.

168. Again, after I had thus considered the sins of the saints in particular, and found that mine went beyond them, I began to think this way with myself: Suppose I should put all theirs together, and mine alone against them, might I not then find some encouragement? For if mine, though bigger than any one of theirs, should yet be only equal to all of them, then there is hope; for the blood that has power enough in it to wash away all theirs has power enough in it to do away mine, though this one were fully as big as all theirs, if not bigger. Here again I would consider the sin of David, of Solomon, of Manasseh, of Peter, and the rest of the great offenders; and I would also labor, as far as I fairly could, to aggravate and heighten their sins by various circumstances.

169. I would think to myself that David shed blood to cover his adultery, and that by the sword of the children of Ammon, a work that could not be done except by continued, deliberate contrivance, which was a great aggravation of his sin. But then this would turn upon me: Ah! but these were only sins against the law, from which a Jesus was sent to save them; but yours is a sin against the Savior, and who shall save you from that?

170. Then I thought of Solomon, and how he sinned in loving foreign women, in falling away to their idols, in building them temples, in doing this after light, in his old age, after great mercy received. But the same conclusion that cut me off in the former consideration cut me off as to this, namely, that all those were only sins against the law, for which God had provided a remedy; but I had sold my Savior, and there now remained no more sacrifice for sin.

171. I would then add to these men’s sins the sins of Manasseh: how he built altars for idols in the house of the Lord; he also observed omens, used enchantments, had dealings with wizards, was a wizard, had his familiar spirits, burned his children in the fire in sacrifice to devils, and made the streets of Jerusalem run down with the blood of innocents. These, I thought, are great sins, sins of a bloody color; but yet it would turn upon me again: “None of them is of the nature of yours; you have parted with Jesus, you have sold your Savior.”

172. This one consideration would always kill my heart: “My sin was point-blank against my Savior”; and that too to such a height that I had said of Him in my heart, “Let Him go if He will.” Oh, it seemed to me that this sin was bigger than the sins of a country, of a kingdom, or of the whole world; no one pardonable sin, nor all of them together, was able to equal mine; mine surpassed every one of them.

173. Now I would feel my mind flee from God, as from the face of a dreadful judge; yet this was my torment, that I could not escape His hand: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb 10:31). But blessed be His grace, that scripture, in these fleeing fits, would call as if running after me: “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you” (Isa 44:22). This, I say, would come in upon my mind when I was fleeing from the face of God; for I did flee from His face, that is, my mind and spirit fled before Him; because of His highness I could not endure Him. Then the text would cry, “Return to Me”; it would cry aloud with a very great voice, “Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.” Indeed, this would make me stop a little, and, as it were, look over my shoulder behind me, to see whether I could discern that the God of grace was following me with a pardon in His hand. But no sooner could I do that than all would be clouded and darkened again by that sentence, “For you+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” So I could not return, but fled, though at times it cried, “Return, return,” as if it were calling out after me. But I feared to take hold of it, lest it should not come from God; for that other, as I said, was always sounding in my conscience, “For you+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected,” and so on.

174. Once, as I was walking to and fro in a good man’s shop, bemoaning myself in my sad and doleful state, afflicting myself with self-abhorrence for this wicked and ungodly thought, lamenting also this hard lot of mine, that I should commit so great a sin, greatly fearing I would not be pardoned, and praying also in my heart that, if this sin of mine differed from the sin against the Holy Spirit, the Lord would show it to me; and being now ready to sink with fear, suddenly there was, as if it had rushed in at the window, the noise of wind upon me, but very pleasant, and as if I had heard a voice speaking: “Did you ever refuse to be justified by the blood of Christ?” And with that my whole past life as a professing Christian was in a moment opened to me, and in it I was made to see that I had not done so on purpose; so my heart answered, groaning, “No.” Then that word of God fell upon me with power: “See that you+ do not refuse Him who speaks” (Heb 12:25). This made a strange seizure upon my spirit; it brought light with it, and commanded a silence in my heart of all those tumultuous thoughts that before, like masterless hell-hounds, used to roar and bellow and make a hideous noise within me. It showed me also that Jesus Christ still had a word of grace and mercy for me, that He had not, as I had feared, quite forsaken and cast off my soul; yes, this was a kind of chiding for my proneness to desperation, a kind of threatening of me if I did not, notwithstanding my sins and their heinousness, venture my salvation upon the Son of God. But as to my judging about this strange dispensation, what it was I do not know, nor do I know where it came from. I have not yet, in twenty years’ time, been able to make a judgment of it; I thought then what I would be loath to speak here. But truly, that sudden rushing wind was as if an angel had come upon me; but both it and the greeting I will leave until the day of judgment. Only this I say: it commanded a great calm in my soul; it persuaded me there might be hope; it showed me, as I thought, what the unpardonable sin was, and that my soul still had the blessed privilege of fleeing to Jesus Christ for mercy. But, I say, concerning this dispensation, I do not yet know what to say about it; and this was also, in truth, the reason that at first I did not speak of it in the book. I now also leave it to be thought on by men of sound judgment. I do not lay the weight of my salvation on it, but on the Lord Jesus, in the promise; yet, seeing I am here unfolding my secret things, I thought it might not be altogether unfitting to let this also show itself, though I cannot now relate the matter as I experienced it there. This lasted, in the savor of it, for about three or four days, and then I began to mistrust and to despair again.

175. So my life still hung in doubt before me, not knowing which way I should tip; only this I found my soul desire, even to cast itself at the foot of grace, by prayer and supplication. But oh! it was hard for me now to have the face to pray to this Christ for mercy, against whom I had most vilely sinned in this way; it was hard work, I say, to venture to look Him in the face against whom I had so vilely sinned; and indeed, I have found it as difficult to come to God by prayer, after backsliding from Him, as to do anything else. Oh, the shame that now came over me! especially when I thought, I am now going to pray to Him for mercy whom I had so lightly esteemed only a little while before! I was ashamed, yes, even confounded, because this villainy had been committed by me; but I saw that there was only one way for me: I must go to Him and humble myself before Him, and beg that He, of His wonderful mercy, would show pity to me, and have mercy on my wretched, sinful soul.

176. When the tempter saw this, he strongly suggested to me that I ought not to pray to God, for prayer was not for anyone in my case, nor could it do me any good, because I had rejected the Mediator, by whom all prayers came with acceptance to God the Father, and without whom no prayer could come into His presence. “So now to pray is only to add sin to sin; yes, now to pray, seeing God has cast you off, is the most direct way to anger and offend Him more than you ever did before.”

177. “For God,” he said, “has been weary of you these several years already, because you are not one of His; your bawlings in His ears have been no pleasant voice to Him; and therefore He let you sin this sin, that you might be quite cut off; and will you still pray?” This the devil urged, and he set before me how, in Numbers, Moses said to the children of Israel that because they would not go up to possess the land when God wanted them to, therefore He barred them out of it forever after, though they prayed with tears that they might go in (Num 14:36, 37, etc.).

178. As it is said in another place (Exod 21:14), the man who sins presumptuously shall be taken from God’s altar, that he may die; just as Joab was by King Solomon, when he thought to find shelter there (1 Kgs 2:28, etc.). These places pinched me very sorely; yet, my case being desperate, I thought to myself, I can only die; and if it must be so, it shall be said of me once, “Such a one died at the foot of Christ in prayer.” This I did, but with great difficulty, God knows; and that because, together with this, that saying about Esau would continually be set at my heart, like a flaming sword, to keep the way of the tree of life, lest I should take of it and live. Oh! who knows how hard I found it to come to God in prayer?

179. I also desired the prayers of the people of God for me, but I feared that God would give them no heart to do it; yes, I trembled in my soul to think that one or another of them would soon tell me that God had said to them the words He once said to the prophet concerning the children of Israel, “Do not pray for this people, for I have rejected them” (Jer 11:14). So: “Do not pray for him, for I have rejected him.” Yes, I thought that He had whispered this to some of them already, only they dared not tell me so, nor dared I ask them about it, for fear that, if it were so, it would drive me quite out of my mind. “Man knows the beginning of sin,” said Spira, “but who sets bounds to where it will end?”

180. About this time I took an opportunity to open my mind to an old Christian, and told him my whole case; I told him also that I was afraid I had sinned the sin against the Holy Spirit; and he told me he thought so too. Here, therefore, I had only cold comfort; but, talking a little more with him, I found him, though a good man, a stranger to much combat with the devil. So I went to God again, as well as I could, for mercy still.

181. Now also the tempter began to mock me in my misery, saying that, since I had parted with the Lord Jesus in this way, and provoked Him to displeasure, who would have stood between my soul and the flame of devouring fire, there was now only one way left, and that was to pray that God the Father would be the Mediator between His Son and me, that we might be reconciled again, and that I might have that blessed benefit in Him which His blessed saints enjoyed.

182. Then that scripture seized on my soul, “He is of one mind, and who can turn Him?” Oh! I saw it was as easy to persuade Him to make a new world, a new covenant, or a new Bible, besides the one we have already, as to pray for such a thing. This would be to persuade Him that what He had already done was sheer folly, and to plead with Him to alter, yes, to annul, the whole way of salvation; and then that saying would tear my soul apart, “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

183. Now the most free, and full, and gracious words of the gospel were the greatest torment to me; yes, nothing afflicted me so much as the thoughts of Jesus Christ, the remembrance of a Savior; because I had cast Him off, it brought to mind the villainy of my sin and my loss by it; nothing pricked my conscience like this. Every time I thought of the Lord Jesus, of His grace, love, goodness, kindness, gentleness, meekness, death, blood, promises and blessed exhortations, comforts and consolations, it went to my soul like a sword; for continually, alongside these my considerations of the Lord Jesus, these thoughts would make a place for themselves in my heart: “Yes, this is the Jesus, the loving Savior, the Son of God, whom you have parted with, whom you have slighted, despised, and abused. This is the only Savior, the only Redeemer, the only one who could so love sinners as to wash them from their sins in His own most precious blood; but you have no part or lot in this Jesus. You have put Him from you; you have said in your heart, ‘Let Him go if He will.’ Now, therefore, you are severed from Him; you have severed yourself from Him. See, then, His goodness, but see yourself to be no partaker of it.” Oh, thought I, what have I lost! What have I parted with! What have I disinherited my poor soul of! Oh! it is sad to be destroyed by the grace and mercy of God; to have the Lamb, the Savior, turn lion and destroyer (Rev 6). I also trembled, as I have said, at the sight of the saints of God, especially at those who greatly loved Him, and who made it their business to walk continually with Him in this world; for they, in their words, their conduct, and all their expressions of tenderness and fear of sinning against their precious Savior, condemned my soul, laid guilt on it, and added continual affliction and shame to it. The dread of them was upon me, and I trembled at God’s Samuels (1 Sam 16:4).

184. Now also the tempter began afresh to mock my soul another way, saying that Christ indeed pitied my case, and was sorry for my loss; but since I had sinned and transgressed as I had done, He could by no means help me, nor save me from what I feared; for my sin was not of the nature of theirs for whom He bled and died, nor was it counted with those that were laid to His charge when He hung on the tree. Therefore, unless He should come down from heaven and die anew for this sin, though He did indeed greatly pity me, yet I could have no benefit from Him. These things may seem ridiculous to others, even as ridiculous as they were in themselves, but to me they were most tormenting thoughts; every one of them increased my misery: that Jesus Christ should have so much love as to pity me when yet He could not help me. Nor did I think that the reason why He could not help me was that His merits were weak, or His grace and salvation already spent on others, but because His faithfulness to His threatening would not let Him extend His mercy to me. Besides, I thought, as I have already hinted, that my sin was not within the bounds of that pardon that was wrapped up in a promise; and if not, then I knew assuredly that it was easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for me to have eternal life. So the ground of all these fears of mine arose from a steadfast belief that I had in the stability of the holy Word of God, and also from my being misinformed about the nature of my sin.

185. But oh! how this would add to my affliction, to imagine that I should be guilty of such a sin, for which He did not die. These thoughts would so confound me, and imprison me, and tie me up from faith, that I did not know what to do; but oh! thought I, if only He would come down again! Oh, if only the work of man’s redemption were yet to be done by Christ! How I would pray Him and entreat Him to count and reckon this sin among the rest for which He died! But this scripture would strike me down as dead, “Since Christ was raised from the dead, He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him” (Rom 6:9).

186. So, by the strange and unusual assaults of the tempter, my soul, like a broken vessel, was driven as with the winds, and tossed at times headlong into despair, at times onto the covenant of works, and at times to wishing that the new covenant and its conditions might, so far as I thought myself concerned, be turned another way and changed. But in all these I was only like those who dash against the rocks; more broken, scattered, and torn. Oh, the unthought-of imaginations, frights, fears, and terrors that are brought about by a thorough application of guilt, yielding to desperation! This is the man who has his dwelling “in the tombs” with the dead; that is, always “crying out and cutting himself with stones” (Mark 5:2–5). But I say, all in vain; desperation will not comfort him, the old covenant will not save him; no, heaven and earth shall pass away before one jot or tittle of the Word and law of grace shall fail or be removed. This I saw, this I felt, and under this I groaned; yet this advantage I gained by it, namely, a further confirmation of the certainty of the way of salvation, and that the Scriptures were the Word of God! Oh! I cannot now express what I then saw and felt of the steadiness of Jesus Christ, the rock of man’s salvation; what was done could not be undone, added to, or altered. I saw, indeed, that sin might drive the soul beyond Christ, even the sin which is unpardonable; but woe to him who was so driven, for the Word would shut him out.

187. So I was always sinking, whatever I thought or did. One day I walked to a neighboring town, and sat down on a bench in the street, and fell into a very deep pause about the most fearful state my sin had brought me to; and, after long musing, I lifted up my head, but it seemed to me as if the sun that shines in the heavens grudged to give light, and as if the very stones in the street, and the tiles on the houses, bent themselves against me; it seemed to me that they all combined together to banish me out of the world; I was abhorred by them, and unfit to dwell among them, or to be partaker of their benefits, because I had sinned against the Savior. Oh, how much happier now was every created thing than I was! for they stood fast and kept their station, but I was gone and lost.

188. Then, breaking out in the bitterness of my soul, I said to myself, with a grievous sigh, “How can God comfort such a wretch as I?” I had no sooner said it than this returned upon me, as an echo answers a voice, “This sin does not lead to death.” At this I was as if I had been raised out of a grave, and cried out again, “Lord, how could You find such a word as this?” For I was filled with wonder at the fitness, and also at the unexpectedness, of the sentence; the fitness of the word, the rightness of its timing, the power, and sweetness, and light, and glory that came with it, were also marvelous for me to find. I was now, for the time, out of doubt about that which I had been so much in doubt about before; my fears before were that my sin was not pardonable, and so that I had no right to pray, to repent, and so on, or that if I did, it would be of no advantage or profit to me. But now, thought I, if this sin does not lead to death, then it is pardonable; so from this I have encouragement to come to God, by Christ, for mercy, and to consider the promise of forgiveness as that which stands with open arms to receive me, as well as others. This, therefore, was a great easing to my mind; that is, that my sin was pardonable, that it was not the sin leading to death (1 John 5:16, 17). None but those who know by their own experience what my trouble was can tell what relief came to my soul from this consideration; it was a release from my former bonds, and a shelter from the former storm. I seemed now to stand on the same ground as other sinners, and to have as good a right to the word and to prayer as any of them.

189. Now, I say, I had hopes that my sin was not unpardonable, but that there might be hope for me to obtain forgiveness. But oh, how Satan now laid about him to bring me down again! But he could by no means do it, neither that day nor most of the next, for this good sentence stood like a mill-post at my back; yet, toward the evening of the next day, I felt this word begin to leave me and to withdraw its support from me, and so I returned to my old fears again, but with a great deal of grudging and peevishness, for I feared the sorrow of despair; nor could my faith any longer retain this word.

190. But the next day, at evening, being under many fears, I went to seek the Lord; and as I prayed, I cried, and my soul cried to Him in these words, with strong cries: “O Lord, I beg You, show me that You have loved me with an everlasting love” (Jer 31:3). I had no sooner said it than, with sweetness, this returned upon me, as an echo or sounding again, “I have loved you with an everlasting love.” Now I went to bed in quiet; also, when I woke the next morning, it was fresh upon my soul, and I believed it.

191. But even so the tempter did not leave me; for it could not have been fewer than a hundred times that he labored that day to break my peace. Oh! the combats and conflicts that I then met with as I strove to hold on to this word; that of Esau would fly in my face like lightning. At times I would be up and down twenty times in an hour, yet God bore me up and kept my heart on this word, from which I also had, for several days together, very much sweetness and comforting hopes of pardon; for this is how it was made plain to me: “I loved you while you were committing this sin, I loved you before, I love you still, and I will love you forever.”

192. Yet I saw my sin as most barbarous, and a filthy crime, and could not help concluding, and that with great shame and astonishment, that I had horribly abused the holy Son of God; so I felt my soul greatly love and pity Him, and my heart yearn toward Him; for I saw He was still my Friend, and rewarded me good for evil; yes, the love and affection that then burned within me toward my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ worked, at this time, such a strong and hot desire for revenge on myself for the abuse I had done to Him, that, to speak as I then thought, had I had a thousand gallons of blood in my veins, I could freely have spilled it all then at the command and feet of this my Lord and Savior.

193. And as I was thus musing and deep in thought, considering how to love the Lord and to express my love to Him, that saying came in upon me, “If You, O Lord, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared” (Ps 130:3, 4). These were good words to me, especially the latter part; that is, that there is forgiveness with the Lord, that He might be feared; that is, as I then understood it, that He might be loved and held in reverence; for it was made plain to me in this way: that the great God set so high a value on the love of His poor creatures that, rather than go without their love, He would pardon their transgressions.

194. And now that word was fulfilled in me, and I was also refreshed by it, “Then they shall be ashamed and confounded, and never again open their mouth because of their shame, when I am pacified toward them for all they have done, declares the Lord God” (Ezek 16:63). So my soul at this time, and, as I then thought, forever, was set free from being afflicted with my former guilt and dismay.

195. But before many weeks were over I began to lose heart again, fearing that, in spite of all I had enjoyed, I might yet be deceived and destroyed at the last; for this consideration came strongly into my mind: that whatever comfort and peace I thought I might have from the word of the promise of life, yet unless my refreshment could be found to have the concurrence and agreement of the Scriptures, let me think what I would of it, and hold it ever so fast, I should find no such thing at the end; “for Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35).

196. Now my heart began again to ache and fear that I might meet with disappointment at the last; so I began, with all seriousness, to examine my former comfort, and to consider whether one who had sinned as I had done might with confidence trust in the faithfulness of God, laid down in those words by which I had been comforted and on which I had leaned. But now those sayings were brought to my mind, “For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, if they fall away, to renew them again to repentance” (Heb 6:4–6). “For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sin, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume the adversaries” (Heb 10:26, 27). Even “like Esau, who for one morsel of food sold his birthright. For you+ know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears” (Heb 12:16, 17).

197. Now the word of the gospel was forced from my soul, so that no promise or encouragement was to be found in the Bible for me; and now that saying would work on my spirit to afflict me, “Do not rejoice, O Israel, with exultation like the nations” (Hos 9:1). For I saw indeed there was cause of rejoicing for those who held to Jesus; but as for me, I had cut myself off by my transgressions, and left myself neither foothold nor handhold among all the stays and props in the precious word of life.

198. And truly I now felt myself sink into a gulf, like a house whose foundation is destroyed; I likened myself, in this condition, to the case of some child that had fallen into a mill-pit, who, though it could make some shift to scrabble and sprawl in the water, yet because it could find no hold for hand or foot, must at last die in that condition. As soon as this fresh assault had fastened on my soul, that scripture came into my heart, “This is for many days” (Dan 10:14). And indeed I found it was so; for I could not be delivered, nor brought to peace again, until nearly two and a half years were completely finished. So these words, though in themselves they tended to discouragement, yet to me, who feared this condition would be eternal, were at times a help and refreshment.

199. For, thought I, many days are not forever, many days will have an end; therefore, seeing I was to be afflicted, not a few, but many days, yet I was glad it was only for many days. In this way, I say, I could at times bring myself back and give myself some help, for as soon as ever the words first came into my mind, I knew my trouble would be long; yet this would be only at times, for I could not always think on this, nor always be helped by it, even when I did.

200. Now while these scriptures lay before me, and laid sin anew at my door, that saying in the eighteenth of Luke, with others, encouraged me to pray. Then the tempter again laid at me very sorely, suggesting that neither the mercy of God nor the blood of Christ concerned me at all, nor could they help me for my sin; therefore it was only in vain to pray. Yet, thought I, “I will pray.” “But,” said the tempter, “your sin is unpardonable.” “Well,” said I, “I will pray.” “It is no use,” said he. “Yet,” said I, “I will pray.” So I went to prayer to God; and while I was at prayer, I spoke words to this effect: “Lord, Satan tells me that neither Your mercy nor Christ’s blood is sufficient to save my soul. Lord, shall I honor You most by believing You will and can? or him, by believing You neither will nor can? Lord, I would gladly honor You by believing You will and can.”

201. And as I was thus before the Lord, that scripture fastened on my heart, “O man, your faith is great” (Matt 15:28), as if someone had clapped me on the back as I was on my knees before God. Yet I was not able to believe this, that this was a prayer of faith, till almost six months after; for I could not think that I had faith, or that there should be a word for me to act faith on; therefore I would continually be as one sticking in the jaws of desperation, and went mourning up and down in a sad condition, crying, “Is His mercy clean gone? Is His mercy clean gone forever?” And I thought at times, even when I was groaning out these words, that they seemed to make a question of whether it was or not; yet I greatly feared it was.

202. There was nothing I now longed for more than to be put out of doubt about this question; and, as I was earnestly desiring to know if there was indeed hope for me, these words came rolling into my mind, “Will the Lord cast off forever and never show His favor again? Is His mercy clean gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has He in anger shut up His tender mercies?” (Ps 77:7–9). And all the while they ran in my mind, I thought I continually had this as the answer: “It is a question whether He has or not; it may be He has not.” Yes, the question seemed to me to carry in it a sure affirmation that indeed He had not, nor would so cast off, but would show favor; that His promise does not fail, and that He had not forgotten to be gracious, nor would in anger shut up His tender mercies. There was also something on my heart at the same time which I cannot now call to mind, which, with this text, sweetened my heart, and made me conclude that His mercy might not be quite gone, nor clean gone forever.

203. At another time, I remember, I was again much under this question, “Is the blood of Christ sufficient to save my soul?” In this doubt I continued from morning till about seven or eight at night; and at last, when I was, as it were, quite worn out with fear that it would not lay hold on me, these words suddenly sounded within my heart, “He is able.” But it seemed to me this word able was spoken loudly to me; it showed a great word, it seemed to be written in great letters, and gave such a jolt to my fear and doubt (I mean for the time it stayed with me, which was about a day) as I never had from that in all my life, either before or after (Heb 7:25).

204. But one morning, when I was again at prayer, and trembling under the fear that no word of God could help me, that piece of a sentence darted in upon me, “My grace is sufficient.” At this I thought I felt some stay, as if there might be hope. But oh, how good a thing it is for God to send His word! For about a fortnight before, I was looking at this very place, and then I thought it could not come near my soul with comfort; so I threw down my book in a fit of temper. Then I thought it was not large enough for me; no, not large enough; but now it was as if it had arms of grace so wide that it could enclose not only me, but many more such as I besides.

205. By these words I was sustained, yet not without exceeding conflicts, for the space of seven or eight weeks; for my peace would be in it and out, at times twenty times a day; comfort now, and trouble a moment later; peace now, and before I could go a furlong as full of fear and guilt as ever heart could hold; and this was not only now and then, but my whole seven weeks’ experience; for this about the sufficiency of grace, and that about Esau’s parting with his birthright, would be like a pair of scales within my mind; sometimes one end would be uppermost, and sometimes again the other; and according to which it was would be my peace or trouble.

206. So I continually prayed to God that He would come in with this scripture more fully on my heart; that is, that He would help me to apply the whole sentence, for as yet I could not. What He gave, I gathered; but further I could not go, for as yet it only helped me to hope there might be mercy for me, “My grace is sufficient”; and though it went no further, it answered my former question, namely, that there was hope; yet, because “for you” was left out, I was not content, but prayed to God for that also. So one day, as I was in a meeting of God’s people, full of sadness and terror, for my fears were strong upon me again, and as I was now thinking my soul was never the better, but my case most sad and fearful, these words suddenly broke in upon me with great power, “My grace is sufficient for you, my grace is sufficient for you, my grace is sufficient for you,” three times together; and oh! I thought that every word was a mighty word to me, as “my,” and “grace,” and “sufficient,” and “for you”; they were then, and at times still are, far bigger than others are.

207. At that time my understanding was so enlightened that it was as though I had seen the Lord Jesus look down from heaven through the tiles upon me, and direct these words to me. This sent me home mourning; it broke my heart, and filled me full of joy, and laid me as low as the dust; only it did not stay long with me, I mean in this glory and refreshing comfort, yet it continued with me for several weeks, and encouraged me to hope. But as soon as that powerful working of it was taken off my heart, that other saying about Esau returned upon me as before; so my soul hung as in a pair of scales again, sometimes up and sometimes down, now in peace, and soon again in terror.

208. So I went on for many weeks, sometimes comforted, and sometimes tormented; and especially at some times my torment would be very sore, for all those scriptures named before in Hebrews would be set before me, as the only sentences that would keep me out of heaven. Then again I would begin to repent that that thought ever went through me; I would also think this way with myself, “Why, how many scriptures are there against me? There are only three or four; and cannot God miss them, and save me in spite of them all?” At times, again, I would think, “Oh! if it were not for these three or four words, how I might be comforted now!” And I could hardly keep myself, at some times, from wishing them out of the book.

209. Then it seemed to me as if both Peter, and Paul, and John, and all the writers, looked on me with scorn and held me in derision; and as if they said to me, “All our words are truth, one of as much force as another. It is not we who have cut you off, but you have cast yourself away; there is none of our sentences that you must take hold of but these, and such as these: ‘It is impossible’; ‘there remains no more sacrifice for sin’ (Heb 6). And ‘it would have been better for them not to have known’ the will of God ‘than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them’ (2 Pet 2:21). ‘For Scripture cannot be broken.’”

210. These, like the elders of the city of refuge, I saw were to be the judges both of my case and of me, while I stood, with the avenger of blood at my heels, trembling at their gate for deliverance; also, with a thousand fears and mistrusts, I feared that they would shut me out forever (Josh 20:3, 4).

211. So I was confounded, not knowing what to do, nor how to be satisfied in this question, “Could the Scriptures agree in the salvation of my soul?” I quaked at the apostles; I knew their words were true, and that they must stand forever.

212. And I remember one day, as I was in various frames of spirit, and considering that these frames were always according to the nature of the separate scriptures that came in upon my mind: if it was this one of grace, then I was quiet; but if that one of Esau, then I was tormented. “Lord,” thought I, “if both these scriptures would meet in my heart at once, I wonder which of them would get the better of me.” So it seemed to me I had a longing mind that they might both come upon me together; yes, I desired of God that they might.

213. Well, about two or three days after, so they did indeed; they bolted upon me both at once, and worked and struggled strangely in me for a while; at last, that about Esau’s birthright began to grow weak, and withdraw, and vanish, and this about the sufficiency of grace prevailed, with peace and joy. And as I was musing about this, that scripture came home to me, “Mercy triumphs over judgment” (Jas 2:13).

214. This was a wonderment to me; yet truly I am inclined to think it was of God; for the word of the law and wrath must give place to the word of life and grace; because, though the word of condemnation is glorious, yet the word of life and salvation far exceeds it in glory (2 Cor 3:8–12; Mark 9:5–7). Also, Moses and Elijah must both vanish, and leave Christ and His saints alone.

215. This scripture also now most sweetly visited my soul, “And him who comes to Me I will by no means cast out” (John 6:37). Oh, the comfort I had from this word, “by no means”! as if to say, in no way, not for anything, whatever he has done. But Satan would labor hard to pull this promise from me, telling me that Christ did not mean me, and such as I, but sinners of a lower rank, who had not done as I had done. But I would answer him again, “Satan, there is no such exception in these words; but ‘him who comes’, him, any him: ‘him who comes to Me I will by no means cast out.’” And I still remember this well, that of all the tricks Satan used to take this scripture from me, he never once put this question, “But do you come aright?” And I have thought the reason was that he thought I knew full well what coming aright was; for I saw that to come aright was to come as I was, a vile and ungodly sinner, and to cast myself at the feet of mercy, condemning myself for sin. If ever Satan and I strove for any word of God in all my life, it was for this good word of Christ; he at one end and I at the other. Oh, what work we made! It was for this in John, I say, that we tugged and strove so; he pulled and I pulled; but, God be praised, I got the better of him, I got some sweetness from it.

216. But notwithstanding all these helps and blessed words of grace, yet that of Esau’s selling his birthright would still at times distress my conscience; for though I had been most sweetly comforted, and that only just before, yet when that came into my mind, it would make me fear again; I could not be quite rid of it; it would be with me every day. So now I went to work another way, namely, to consider the nature of this blasphemous thought; I mean, if I should take the words at their largest, and give them their own natural force and scope, every word in them. When I had considered them this way, I found that if they were fairly taken, they would amount to this: that I had freely left the Lord Jesus Christ to His choice, whether He would be my Savior or not; for the wicked words were these, “Let Him go if He will.” Then that scripture gave me hope, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you” (Heb 13:5). “O Lord,” said I, “but I have left You.” Then it answered again, “But I will not leave you.” For this I thank God also.

217. Yet I was grievously afraid He would, and found it exceedingly hard to trust Him, seeing I had so offended Him. I would have been exceedingly glad if this thought had never befallen me, for then I thought I could, with much more ease and freedom, have leaned on His grace. I see it was with me as it was with Joseph’s brothers; the guilt of their own wickedness often filled them with fears that their brother would at last despise them (Gen 50:15–17).

218. Yet above all the scriptures that I had yet met with, that in the twentieth of Joshua was the greatest comfort to me, which speaks of the slayer who was to flee for refuge. “And if the avenger of blood pursues the slayer, then,” says Moses, “those who are the elders of the city of refuge shall not deliver him into his hand, because he struck his neighbor unwittingly, and did not hate him beforehand.” Oh, blessed be God for this word; I was convinced that I was the slayer; and that the avenger of blood pursued me, I felt with great terror; only now it remained for me to inquire whether I had a right to enter the city of refuge. So I found that he must not enter who lay in wait to shed blood: it was not the willful murderer, but he who did it unwittingly, he who did it unawares; not out of spite, or grudge, or malice; he who shed it unwittingly, even he who did not hate his neighbor before. Therefore:

219. I thought surely I was the man who must enter, because I had struck my neighbor unwittingly, and did not hate him beforehand. I did not hate Him beforehand; no, I prayed to Him, and was tender of sinning against Him; yes, and against this wicked temptation I had striven for a year before; yes, and also when it did pass through my heart, it did so in spite of all I could do. So I thought I had a right to enter this city, and the elders, who are the apostles, were not to deliver me up. This, therefore, was a great comfort to me, and gave me much ground of hope.

220. Yet being very exacting, for my pain had made me so that I did not know what ground was firm enough to bear me, I had one question that my soul greatly desired to be satisfied about, and that was, “Is it possible for any soul that has indeed sinned the unpardonable sin to receive after that even the least true spiritual comfort from God through Christ?” After I had considered it much, I found the answer was, No, they could not; and that for these reasons:

221. First, because those who have sinned that sin are barred from a share in the blood of Christ, and being shut out of that, they must be without the least ground of hope, and so of spiritual comfort; for to such “there remains no more sacrifice for sin” (Heb 10:26). Secondly, because they are denied a share in the promise of life; they shall never be forgiven, “neither in this world nor in the world to come” (Matt 12:32). Thirdly, the Son of God also excludes them from a share in His blessed intercession, being forever ashamed to acknowledge them both before His holy Father and the blessed angels in heaven (Mark 8:38).

222. When I had considered this matter with much deliberation, and could not but conclude that the Lord had comforted me, and that too after this wicked sin of mine, then I thought I dared venture to come near those most fearful and terrible scriptures with which all this while I had been so greatly frightened. Before this I had scarcely dared cast my eye on them; indeed, a hundred times I could hardly keep from wishing them out of the Bible, for I thought they would destroy me. But now, I say, I began to take some measure of encouragement to come close to them, to read them and consider them, and to weigh their scope and tendency.

223. When I began to do this, I found their face changed; for they did not look so grim as I had thought they did before. And first, I came to the sixth of Hebrews, still trembling for fear it would strike me. When I had considered it, I found that the falling there intended was a falling quite away; that is, as I understood it, a falling from, and an absolute denying of, the gospel of the forgiveness of sins by Christ; for the apostle begins his argument from these (vv. 1–3). Secondly, I found that this falling away must be done openly, even in the view of the world, even so as “to put Christ to an open shame.” Thirdly, I found that those he there intended were forever shut up by God, in blindness, hardness, and impenitence: it is “impossible they should be renewed again to repentance.” By all these particulars I found, to God’s everlasting praise, that my sin was not the sin intended in this place.

First, I confessed I was fallen, but not fallen away, that is, from the profession of faith in Jesus to eternal life.

Secondly, I confessed that I had put Jesus Christ to shame by my sin, but not to open shame; I did not deny Him before men, nor condemn Him as a fruitless one before the world.

Thirdly, nor did I find that God had shut me up, or refused to let me come, though I found it hard work indeed to come to Him by sorrow and repentance. Blessed be God for unsearchable grace.

224. Then I considered the passage in the tenth of Hebrews, and found that the willful sin mentioned there is not every willful sin, but that sin which throws off Christ, and then His commandments too. Secondly, it must also be done openly, before two or three witnesses, to answer to what the law required (v. 28). Thirdly, this sin cannot be committed except with great insult done to the Spirit of grace, despising both the warnings against that sin and the persuasions to the contrary. But the Lord knows that, though this sin of mine was devilish, it did not amount to these.

225. And as for the passage in the twelfth of Hebrews, about Esau’s selling his birthright, though this was what had killed me, and stood like a spear against me, yet now I considered: First, that his was not a hasty thought against the continual labor of his mind, but a thought consented to and put into practice as well, and that too after some deliberation (Gen 25). Secondly, it was a public and open action, before his brother at least, if not before many more; this made his sin of a far more heinous nature than it would otherwise have been. Thirdly, he continued to slight his birthright: “He ate and drank and then got up and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright” (v. 34). Indeed, twenty years after, he was found to despise it still: “And Esau said, ‘I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what belongs to you’” (Gen 33:9).

226. Now as to this, that Esau sought a place of repentance, this is what I thought. First, this was not for the birthright, but for the blessing; this is clear from the apostle, and Esau himself makes the distinction: “He took my birthright” (that is, formerly), “and now he has taken my blessing” (Gen 27:36). Secondly, having considered this, I came again to the apostle, to see what might be the mind of God, in a New Testament style and sense, concerning Esau’s sin. So far as I could understand, this was the mind of God: that the birthright signified regeneration, and the blessing the eternal inheritance. For so the apostle seems to hint: “Lest there be any profane person, like Esau, who for one morsel of food sold his birthright”; as if he should say, Lest there be any person among you who casts off all those blessed beginnings of God that are now upon him, tending to a new birth, lest they become like Esau, and be rejected afterward, when they want to inherit the blessing.

227. For there are many who, in the day of grace and mercy, despise those things which are indeed the birthright to heaven, who yet, when the deciding day appears, will cry as loud as Esau, “Lord, Lord, open to us.” But then, as Isaac would not change his mind, no more will God the Father, but will say, “I have blessed these, and indeed, they will be blessed; but as for you+, depart, you+ are workers of iniquity” (Gen 27:33; Luke 13:25–27).

228. When I had considered these scriptures in this way, and found that to understand them so was not against other scriptures but in agreement with them, this added still further to my encouragement and comfort. It also gave a great blow to that objection, namely, that the Scriptures could not agree in the salvation of my soul. And now only the tail end of the tempest remained, for the thunder had gone beyond me; only some drops still remained, which now and then would fall on me. But because my former frights and anguish had been very sore and deep, it often happened to me still, as it happens to those who have been scared by fire, that I thought every voice was “Fire! fire!” Every little touch would hurt my tender conscience.

229. But one day, as I was passing through the field, and that too with some blows upon my conscience, fearing that all was still not right, suddenly this sentence fell upon my soul: “Your righteousness is in heaven.” And I thought, along with it, that I saw with the eyes of my soul Jesus Christ at God’s right hand. There, I say, was my righteousness; so that wherever I was, or whatever I was doing, God could not say of me, “He lacks My righteousness,” for that was right before Him. I also saw, moreover, that it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor yet my bad frame that made my righteousness worse; for my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself, “the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb 13:8).

230. Now my chains did indeed fall off my legs; I was loosed from my afflictions and irons; my temptations also fled away. So from that time those dreadful scriptures of God left off troubling me. Now I also went home rejoicing for the grace and love of God. So when I came home, I looked to see if I could find that sentence, “Your righteousness is in heaven,” but could not find such a saying, and so my heart began to sink again. Only this was brought to my remembrance: “He has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.” By this word I saw that the other sentence was true (1 Cor 1:30).

231. For by this scripture I saw that the man Christ Jesus, as He is distinct from us in His bodily presence, is our righteousness and sanctification before God. Here, therefore, I lived for some time, very sweetly at peace with God through Christ. Oh, I thought, Christ! Christ! There was nothing but Christ before my eyes. I was not now only for looking at this and that benefit of Christ separately, such as His blood, burial, or resurrection, but considered Him as a whole Christ! As He in whom all these, and all His other virtues, relations, offices, and works, met together, and that as He sat at the right hand of God in heaven.

232. It was glorious to me to see His exaltation, and the worth and prevailing power of all His benefits, and that because now I could look from myself to Him, and would reckon that all those graces of God that were now green in me were still only like those cracked groats and fourpence-halfpennies that rich men carry in their purses, while their gold is in their trunks at home! Oh, I saw my gold was in my trunk at home! In Christ, my Lord and Savior! Now Christ was all: all my wisdom, all my righteousness, all my sanctification, and all my redemption.

233. Further, the Lord also led me into the mystery of union with the Son of God: that I was joined to Him, that I was flesh of His flesh and bone of His bone; and now that was a sweet word to me in Ephesians 5:30. By this also my faith in Him as my righteousness was the more confirmed in me; for if He and I were one, then His righteousness was mine, His merits mine, His victory also mine. Now I could see myself in heaven and on earth at once: in heaven by my Christ, by my head, by my righteousness and life, though on earth by my body or person.

234. Now I saw that Christ Jesus was looked on by God, and should also be looked on by us, as that common or public person in whom the whole body of His elect are always to be considered and reckoned: that we fulfilled the law by Him, died by Him, rose from the dead by Him, and got the victory over sin, death, the devil, and hell by Him. When He died, we died; and so of His resurrection. “Your dead will live; together with my dead body they will rise,” he says (Isa 26:19). And again, “After two days He will revive us; and on the third day we will live in His presence” (Hos 6:2). This is now fulfilled by the sitting down of the Son of Man at the right hand of the Majesty in the heavens, according to that word to the Ephesians, “He raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus” (Eph 2:6).

235. Ah, these blessed considerations and scriptures, with many others of a like nature, were in those days made to spangle in my eyes, so that I have cause to say, “Hallelujah! Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him in His mighty heavens. Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness” (Ps 150:1, 2).

236. I have thus, in a few words, given you a taste of the sorrow and affliction my soul went through under the guilt and terror that this wicked thought of mine laid on me; and I have also given you a touch of my deliverance from it, and of the sweet and blessed comfort I met with afterward, a comfort which dwelt with my heart for about a year, to my unspeakable wonder. Now, God willing, before I go any further, I will give you in a word or two what I believe was the cause of this temptation, and also, after that, what advantage it became to my soul in the end.

237. As for the causes, I believed they were chiefly two, and of these two I was deeply convinced all the time this trouble lay on me.
