The first was that, when I was delivered from the temptation that went before, I did not continue to pray to God to keep me from temptations that were to come. For though, as I can say in truth, my soul was much in prayer before this trial seized me, yet then I prayed only, or at most chiefly, for the removal of present troubles and for fresh revelations of His love in Christ. This, I saw afterward, was not enough; I should also have prayed that the great God would keep me from the evil that was to come.

238. Of this I was made deeply aware by the prayer of holy David, who, when he was under present mercy, still prayed that God would hold him back from sin and temptation to come. “Then,” he says, “I will be blameless and innocent of the great transgression” (Ps 19:13). By this very word I was galled and condemned, all through this long temptation.

239. Another word that much condemned me for my folly in neglecting this duty was this: “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need” (Heb 4:16). This I had not done, and therefore I was allowed to sin and fall in this way, according to what is written, “Pray that you+ will not enter into temptation.” And truly this very thing lies on me to this day with such weight and awe that, when I come before the Lord, I dare not get up off my knees until I entreat Him for help and mercy against the temptations that are to come. And I beg you, reader, to learn to beware of my negligence, by the afflictions I underwent with sorrow for this very thing, for days, and months, and years.

240. Another cause of this temptation was that I had tempted God, and this is how I did it. Once, when my wife was with child, before her full time had come, her pangs, like those of a woman in labor, were fierce and strong upon her, as if she would immediately have gone into labor and been delivered of an untimely birth. Now it was at this very time that I had been so strongly tempted to question the being of God. So, as my wife lay crying beside me, I said, but with all the secrecy imaginable, only thinking it in my heart, “Lord, if You will now remove this sad affliction from my wife, and cause her to be troubled no more with it this night” (and now her pangs were just upon her), “then I shall know that You can discern the most secret thoughts of the heart.”

241. I had no sooner said it in my heart than her pangs were taken from her, and she was cast into a deep sleep, and so continued till morning. At this I greatly marveled, not knowing what to think; but after I had been awake a good while, and heard her cry no more, I fell asleep too. So when I woke in the morning, it came upon me again, what I had said in my heart the night before, and how the Lord had shown me that He knew my secret thoughts. This was a great astonishment to me for several weeks after.

242. Well, about a year and a half afterward, that wicked, sinful thought of which I have spoken before went through my wicked heart, this very thought: “Let Christ go if He will.” So when I had fallen under guilt for this, the remembrance of my other thought, and of its effect, would also come upon me with this retort, which also carried rebuke along with it: “Now you may see that God does know the most secret thoughts of the heart.”

243. And with this, what passed between the Lord and His servant Gideon fell upon my spirit: how, because Gideon tempted God with his fleece, both wet and dry, when he should have believed and ventured on His word, the Lord afterward tried him by sending him against an innumerable company of enemies, and that too, as far as outward appearance went, without any strength or help (Judg 6–7). So He dealt with me, and justly, for I should have believed His word, and not have put an “if” upon the all-seeingness of God.

244. And now to show you something of the advantages that I have also gained by this temptation. And first, by this I was made continually to possess in my soul a very astonishing sense both of the being and glory of God and of His beloved Son. In the temptation that went before, my soul was perplexed with unbelief, blasphemy, hardness of heart, and questions about the being of God and Christ, the truth of the Word, and the certainty of the world to come; I say, then I was greatly assaulted and tormented with atheism. But now the case was otherwise; now God and Christ were continually before my face, though not in a way of comfort, but in a way of exceeding dread and terror. The glory of the holiness of God at this time broke me to pieces, and the tender heart and compassion of Christ broke me as on the wheel; for I could not consider Him except as a lost and rejected Christ, and the remembrance of this was like the continual breaking of my bones.

245. The Scriptures also were wonderful things to me. I saw that the truth and certainty of them were the keys of the kingdom of heaven: those whom the Scriptures favor they must inherit bliss, but those whom they oppose and condemn must perish forevermore. Oh! this word, “the Scripture cannot be broken,” would tear the caul of my heart; and so would that other, “If you+ forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you+ withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld.” Now I saw the apostles to be the elders of the city of refuge (Josh 20:4): those whom they were to receive in were received to life, but those whom they shut out were to be slain by the avenger of blood.

246. Oh! one sentence of the Scripture afflicted and terrified my mind more (I mean those sentences that stood against me, as at times I thought every one of them did), more, I say, than an army of forty thousand men that might have come against me. Woe to him against whom the Scriptures bend themselves!

247. By this temptation I was made to see more into the nature of the promises than ever I had before. For now I lay trembling under the mighty hand of God, continually torn and rent by the thundering of His justice; and this made me, with an anxious heart and watchful eye, with great fearfulness, turn over every leaf, and with much diligence, mixed with trembling, consider every sentence, together with its natural force and scope.

248. By this temptation, also, I was greatly kept from my former foolish practice of putting aside the word of promise when it came into my mind. For now, though I could not suck that comfort and sweetness from the promise as I had done at other times, yet, like a sinking man, I would catch at all I saw. Formerly I thought I must not lay hold of the promise unless I felt its comfort; but now it was no time to do so, for the avenger of blood pursued me too hard.

249. Now, therefore, I was glad to catch at that word which I still feared I had no ground or right to claim, and even to leap into the bosom of that promise which I still feared shut its heart against me. Now also I would labor to take the Word as God has laid it down, without restraining the natural force of one syllable of it. Oh, what did I now see in that blessed sixth of John, “And him who comes to Me I will by no means cast out” (v. 37). Now I began to consider with myself that God had a bigger mouth to speak with than I had a heart to conceive with. I thought also that He did not speak His words in haste, or in an unadvised heat, but with infinite wisdom and judgment, and in very truth and faithfulness (2 Sam 7:28).

250. In these days, often in my greatest agonies, I would even flounder toward the promise, as horses that are still stuck in the mire flounder toward sound ground, concluding (though as one almost robbed of his wits through fear), On this I will rest and stay, and leave the fulfilling of it to the God of heaven who made it. Oh! many a pull my heart has had with Satan for that blessed sixth of John. I did not now, as at other times, look chiefly for comfort (though, oh, how welcome it would have been to me!), but now a word, a word to lean a weary soul on, that I might not sink forever! That was what I hunted for.

251. Indeed, often when I have been making for the promise, it has seemed to me as if the Lord would refuse my soul forever. It was often as if I had run upon the pikes, and as if the Lord had thrust at me, as with a flaming sword, to keep me from Him. Then I would think of Esther, who went to petition the king contrary to the law (Esth 4:16). I thought also of Benhadad’s servants, who went with ropes upon their heads to their enemies for mercy (1 Kgs 20:31). The woman of Canaan also, who would not be daunted though Christ called her a dog (Matt 15:21–28), and the man who went to borrow bread at midnight (Luke 11:5–8), were great encouragements to me.

252. I never saw those heights and depths in grace, and love, and mercy, as I saw after this temptation. Great sins draw out great grace; and where guilt is most terrible and fierce, there the mercy of God in Christ, when shown to the soul, appears most high and mighty. When Job had passed through his captivity, the Lord “doubled his former possessions” (Job 42:10). Blessed be God for Jesus Christ our Lord. Many other things I might observe here, but I would be brief, and therefore shall omit them at this time; and I pray God that my harms may make others fear to offend, lest they also be made to bear the iron yoke as I did.

I had two or three times, at or about my deliverance from this temptation, such strange perceptions of the grace of God that I could hardly bear up under it; it was so beyond measure amazing, when I thought it could reach me, that I do think, if that sense of it had stayed long upon me, it would have made me unfit for business.

253. Now I shall go on to give you an account of other dealings of the Lord with me, of His dealings with me at various other seasons, and of the temptations I met with then. I shall begin with what I met with when I first joined in fellowship with the people of God in Bedford. After I had proposed to the church that my desire was to walk with them in the order and ordinances of Christ, and was also admitted by them, while I thought of that blessed ordinance of Christ which was His last supper with His disciples before His death, that scripture, “Do this in remembrance of Me” (Luke 22:19), was made a very precious word to me. For by it the Lord came down upon my conscience with the revelation of His death for my sins, and, as I then felt, it was as if He plunged me in its power. But behold, I had not been a partaker at that ordinance long before such fierce and sad temptations attended me at all times in it, both to blaspheme the ordinance and to wish some deadly thing on those who were then eating of it, that, lest I should at any time be guilty of consenting to these wicked and fearful thoughts, I was forced to bend myself all the while to pray to God to keep me from such blasphemies, and also to cry to God to bless the bread and cup to them as it went from mouth to mouth. The reason for this temptation, I have thought since, was that I did not at first approach to partake of it with the reverence that became me.

254. I continued like this for three-quarters of a year, and could never have rest or ease; but at last the Lord came in upon my soul with the same scripture by which my soul had been visited before. And after that I have usually been very well and comforted in partaking of that blessed ordinance, and have, I trust, discerned in it the Lord’s body as broken for my sins, and that His precious blood has been shed for my transgressions.

255. Once I was somewhat inclined to a consumption, and with it, about the spring, I was suddenly and violently seized with much weakness in my outward man, so much that I thought I could not live. Now I began afresh to give myself up to a serious examination of my state and condition for the future, and of my evidences for that blessed world to come. For it has been my usual course, I bless the name of God, always, but especially in the day of affliction, to try to keep my title to the life to come clear before my eyes.

256. But I had no sooner begun to recall to mind my former experience of the goodness of God to my soul than there came flocking into my mind an innumerable company of my sins and transgressions. Among these, the ones that afflicted me most at this time were my deadness, dullness, and coldness in holy duties; my wanderings of heart; my weariness in all good things; my lack of love to God, His ways, and His people; with this at the end of all: “Are these the fruits of Christianity? Are these the tokens of a blessed man?”

257. At the perception of these things my sickness was doubled upon me, for now I was sick in my inward man; my soul was clogged with guilt. Now also all my former experience of God’s goodness to me was quite taken out of my mind, and hidden as if it had never been or been seen. Now my soul was greatly pinched between these two considerations: “Live I must not; die I dare not.” Now I sank and fell in my spirit, and was giving up all for lost. But as I was walking up and down in the house, as a man in a most woeful state, that word of God took hold of my heart, “You+ are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24). But oh, what a turn it made upon me!

258. Now I was like one awakened out of some troublesome sleep and dream, and, listening to this heavenly sentence, it was as if I heard it explained to me like this: “Sinner, you think that because of your sins and infirmities I cannot save your soul; but behold, My Son is by Me, and I look upon Him, and not on you, and will deal with you according as I am pleased with Him.” At this I was greatly lightened in my mind, and made to understand that God could justify a sinner at any time; it was only His looking upon Christ, and imputing His benefits to us, and the work was done at once.

259. And as I was musing like this, that scripture also came with great power upon my spirit, “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy,” etc. (Titus 3:5; 2 Tim 1:9). Now I was raised on high; I saw myself within the arms of grace and mercy. And though before I had been afraid to think of a dying hour, yet now I cried, “Let me die.” Now death was lovely and beautiful in my sight, for I saw that we shall never live indeed till we have gone to the other world. Oh, I thought, this life is only a slumber compared with that above. At this time also I saw more in those words, “heirs of God” (Rom 8:17), than I shall ever be able to express while I live in this world. “Heirs of God”! God Himself is the portion of the saints. This I saw and wondered at, but cannot tell you what I saw.

260. Again, at another time, when I was very ill and weak, all that time also the tempter beset me strongly (for I find he is much for assaulting the soul when it begins to approach the grave; then is his opportunity), laboring to hide from me my former experience of God’s goodness, and also setting before me the terrors of death and the judgment of God. So much so that at this time, through my fear of perishing forever should I die now, I was as one dead before death came, and it was as if I had felt myself already descending into the pit. I thought, I said, that there was no way but that to hell I must go. But behold, just as I was in the midst of those fears, these words of the angels carrying Lazarus into Abraham’s bosom darted in upon me, as if to say, “So it shall be with you when you leave this world.” This sweetly revived my spirit, and helped me to hope in God. When I had mused on this with comfort for a while, that word fell with great weight upon my mind, “O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory?” (1 Cor 15:55). At this I became well in both body and mind at once, for my sickness vanished at once, and I walked comfortably in my work for God again.

261. At another time, though just before I had been fairly well and savory in my spirit, suddenly a great cloud of darkness fell upon me, which so hid from me the things of God and Christ that I was as if I had never seen or known them in my life. I was also so overrun in my soul with a numb, lifeless frame of spirit that I could not feel my soul move or stir after grace and life by Christ; I was as if my loins were broken, or as if my hands and feet had been tied or bound with chains. At this time also I felt some weakness seize upon my outward man, which made the other affliction all the more heavy and uncomfortable to me.

262. After I had been in this condition some three or four days, as I was sitting by the fire, I suddenly felt this word sound in my heart, “I must go to Jesus.” At this my former darkness and atheism fled away, and the blessed things of heaven were set within my view. While I was thus overtaken with surprise so suddenly, “Wife,” I said, “is there ever such a scripture, ‘I must go to Jesus’?” She said she could not tell; so I sat musing still, to see if I could remember such a place. I had not sat more than two or three minutes when this came bolting in upon me, “to myriads of angels,” and with it, Hebrews the twelfth, about Mount Zion, was set before my eyes (vv. 22–24).

263. Then with joy I told my wife, “Oh, now I know, I know!” That night was a good night to me; I have had only a few better. I longed for the company of some of God’s people, that I might have shared with them what God had shown me. Christ was a precious Christ to my soul that night; I could scarcely lie in my bed for joy, and peace, and triumph, through Christ. This great glory did not continue upon me until morning, yet the twelfth chapter of the author to the Hebrews (Heb 12:22–24) was a blessed scripture to me for many days together after this.

264. The words are these: “You+ have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You+ have come to myriads of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You+ have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.” Through this blessed sentence the Lord led me over and over, first to this word, and then to that, and showed me wonderful glory in every one of them. These words also have often since this time been a great refreshment to my spirit. Blessed be God for having mercy on me.

A Brief Account of the Author’s Call to the Work of the Ministry

265. And now that I am telling my experience, I will thrust in here a word or two concerning my preaching of the Word, and of God’s dealing with me in that particular also. For after I had been awakened about five or six years, and helped to see both the need and the worth of Jesus Christ our Lord, and also enabled to venture my soul upon Him, some of the most able among the saints with us (I say the most able for judgment and holiness of life) perceived, as they judged, that God had counted me worthy to understand something of His will in His holy and blessed Word, and had given me utterance, in some measure, to express what I saw to others for their edification. Therefore they asked me, and that with much earnestness, if I would be willing at times to take it in hand, in one of the meetings, to speak a word of exhortation to them.

266. Though at first this much dashed and abashed my spirit, yet being continually asked and entreated by them, I consented to their request, and twice, at two separate assemblies, but in private, though with much weakness and infirmity, I showed my gift among them. At this they not only seemed to be, but solemnly declared, as in the sight of the great God, that they were both moved and comforted, and they gave thanks to the Father of mercies for the grace given to me.

267. After this, at times, when some of them went into the country to teach, they would also want me to go with them. There, though as yet I did not and dared not make use of my gift in an open way, yet more privately, whenever I came among the good people in those places, I sometimes spoke a word of admonition to them also. They received it as the others had, rejoicing at the mercy of God toward me, and declaring that their souls were edified by it.

268. So, to be brief, at last, the church still desiring it, after some solemn prayer to the Lord, with fasting, I was more particularly called forth and appointed to a more regular and public preaching of the Word, not only to and among those who believed, but also to offer the gospel to those who had not yet received the faith of it. About that time I clearly found in my mind a secret pricking forward to it; though, I bless God, not from a desire for vainglory, for at that time I was most sorely afflicted with the fiery darts of the devil concerning my eternal state.

269. But still I could not be content unless I was found in the exercise of my gift. To this I was also greatly spurred on, not only by the continual desires of the godly, but also by that saying of Paul to the Corinthians, “I urge you+, brothers (you+ know the household of Stephanas, that they were the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints), to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer” (1 Cor 16:15, 16).

270. By this text I was made to see that the Holy Spirit never intended that men who have gifts and abilities should bury them in the earth, but rather commanded and stirred up such men to the exercise of their gift, and also commended those who were apt and ready to do so: “They have devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints.” In these days this scripture continually ran in my mind, to encourage and strengthen me in this my work for God. I have also been encouraged by several other scriptures and examples of the godly, both those set down in the Word and in other ancient histories (Acts 8:4; 18:24, 25; 1 Pet 4:10; Rom 12:6; Foxe’s Acts and Monuments).

271. So, though in myself the most unworthy of all the saints, yet I, but with great fear and trembling at the sight of my own weakness, set upon the work, and according to my gift and the proportion of my faith preached that blessed gospel which God had shown me in the holy Word of truth. When the people of the country understood this, they came in by hundreds to hear the Word, and that from all parts, though for many different reasons.

272. And I thank God, He gave me some measure of tender affection and pity for their souls, which also put me forward to labor with great diligence and earnestness to find out such a word as might, if God would bless it, lay hold of and awaken the conscience. In this also the good Lord had regard to the desire of His servant; for I had not preached long before some began to be touched by the Word, and to be greatly afflicted in their minds at the perception of the greatness of their sin and of their need of Jesus Christ.

273. But at first I could not believe that God would speak by me to the heart of any man, as I still counted myself unworthy. Yet those who were touched in this way would love me and have a particular respect for me; and though I refused to believe that they had been awakened by me, they would still confess it and affirm it before the saints of God. They would also bless God for me, unworthy wretch that I am! and count me God’s instrument who showed them the way of salvation.

274. So, seeing them so constant in both their words and deeds, and also so earnestly pressing after the knowledge of Jesus Christ in their hearts, rejoicing that God ever sent me where they were, I began to conclude that it might be so, that God had acknowledged such a foolish one as I in His work. And then that word of God came to my heart with much sweet refreshment, “The blessing of those who were perishing came upon me, and I made the widow’s heart sing for joy” (Job 29:13).

275. At this, therefore, I rejoiced; indeed, the tears of those whom God awakened by my preaching would be both solace and encouragement to me. For I thought of those sayings, “Who is left to cheer me but those whom I have grieved?” (2 Cor 2:2); and again, “Even if I am not an apostle to others, surely I am to you+. For you+ are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord” (1 Cor 9:2). These things, therefore, were another argument to me that God had called me to this work and stood by me in it.

276. In my preaching of the Word, I took special notice of this one thing: that the Lord led me to begin where His Word begins with sinners; that is, to condemn all flesh, and to open up and declare that the curse of God, by the law, belongs to and lays hold on all men as they come into the world, because of sin. Now this part of my work I fulfilled with great feeling; for the terrors of the law, and guilt for my transgressions, lay heavy on my conscience. I preached what I felt, what I smartingly did feel, even that under which my poor soul groaned and trembled to astonishment.

277. Indeed, I have been as one sent to them from the dead; I went myself in chains to preach to them in chains, and carried that fire in my own conscience that I persuaded them to beware of. I can truly say, and that without pretense, that when I have gone to preach, I have gone full of guilt and terror even to the pulpit door, and there it has been taken off, and I have been at liberty in my mind until I have done my work; and then immediately, even before I could get down the pulpit stairs, I have been as bad as I was before. Yet God carried me on, but surely with a strong hand, for neither guilt nor hell could take me off my work.

278. So I went on for the space of two years, crying out against men’s sins and their fearful state because of them. After that the Lord came in upon my own soul with some settled peace and comfort through Christ, for He gave me many sweet revelations of His blessed grace through Him. So now I changed my preaching, for I always preached what I saw and felt. Now, therefore, I labored much to hold forth Jesus Christ in all His offices, relations, and benefits to the world, and strove also to expose, to condemn, and to remove those false supports and props on which the world both leans and by them falls and perishes. On these things also I stayed as long as on the other.

279. After this, God led me into something of the mystery of the union of Christ; so I revealed and showed that to them also. And when I had traveled through these three chief points of the Word of God, over a space of five years or more, I was caught in my present practice and cast into prison, where I have now lain more than as long again, to confirm the truth by way of suffering, as I was before in testifying of it according to the Scriptures by way of preaching.

280. When I have been preaching, I thank God, my heart has often, all through one service and another, cried to God with great earnestness that He would make the Word effectual to the salvation of the soul, being continually grieved lest the enemy should take the Word away from the conscience, and so it should become unfruitful. So I would labor to speak the Word in such a way that by it, if it were possible, the sin and the person guilty of it might be singled out.

281. Also, when I have finished the service, it has gone to my heart to think that the Word should now fall as rain on stony places, and I have continually wished from my heart: “Oh, if only those who have heard me speak this day could see as I do what sin, death, hell, and the curse of God are; and also what the grace, and love, and mercy of God are, through Christ, to men in such a case as theirs, who are still estranged from Him.” And indeed, I often said in my heart before the Lord, “If being hanged up at once before their eyes would be a means to awaken them and confirm them in the truth, I would gladly be contented.”

282. For in my preaching, especially when I have been engaged in the doctrine of life by Christ, without works, it has been as if an angel of God had stood at my back to encourage me. Oh, it has come with such power and heavenly evidence upon my own soul, while I have been laboring to unfold it, to demonstrate it, and to fasten it upon the conscience of others, that I could not be content with saying, “I believe, and am sure”; it seemed to me I was more than sure, if it is lawful to express myself so, that the things I then asserted were true.

283. When I first went out to preach the Word in public, the doctors and priests of the country opened their mouths wide against me. But I was persuaded of this: not to return insult for insult, but to see how many of their carnal professing Christians I could convict of their miserable state by the law, and of their need of Christ and His worth; for I thought, “This will answer for me in time to come, when they stand as my wages before their face” (Gen 30:33).

284. I never cared to meddle with things that were controversial and in dispute among the saints, especially things of the lowest nature; yet it pleased me much to contend with great earnestness for the word of faith and the remission of sins by the death and sufferings of Jesus. But, I say, as to other things, I would let them alone, because I saw they bred strife, and because neither in doing them nor in leaving them undone did they commend us to God as His. Besides, I saw that the work before me ran in another channel, namely, to carry an awakening word; to that, therefore, I stuck and held fast.

285. I never tried to make use of other men’s lines, nor dared to (Rom 15:18), though I do not condemn all who do; for I truly thought, and found by experience, that what was taught me by the Word and Spirit of Christ could be spoken, maintained, and held to by the soundest and best established conscience. And though I will not now say all that I know in this matter, yet my experience has more share in that text of Scripture than many among men are aware (Gal 1:11, 12).

286. If any of those who were awakened by my ministry afterward fell back, as at times too many did, I can truly say their loss has been more to me than if one of my own children, begotten of my body, had been going to its grave. I think, truly, I may say it without any offense to the Lord: nothing has gone so near me as that, unless it was the fear of the loss of the salvation of my own soul. I have counted it as if I had fine buildings and lordships in those places where my children were born. My heart has been so wrapped up in the glory of this excellent work that I counted myself more blessed and honored by God in this than if He had made me the emperor of the Christian world, or the lord of all the glory of the earth without it! Oh, these words: “Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death” (Jas 5:20). “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise” (Prov 11:30). “Then the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever” (Dan 12:3). “After all, who is our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting, if it is not you+ yourselves+ in the presence of our Lord Jesus at His coming? You+ are indeed our glory and our joy” (1 Thess 2:19, 20). These, I say, with many others of a like nature, have been great refreshments to me.

287. I have observed that where I have had a work to do for God, I have first had, as it were, the going of God upon my spirit, to desire that I might preach there. I have also observed that particular souls have been strongly set upon my heart, and I have been stirred up to wish for their salvation; and that these very souls have afterward been given in as the fruits of my ministry. I have observed that a word thrown in by the way has done more work in a sermon than all that was spoken besides. At times, too, when I thought I did no good, then I did the most of all; and at other times, when I thought I would catch them, I have fished for nothing.

288. I have also observed that where there has been a work to do upon sinners, there the devil has begun to roar in the hearts, and by the mouths, of his servants. Yes, often when the wicked world has raged most, there have been souls awakened by the word. I could give particular instances, but I refrain.

289. My great desire in fulfilling my ministry was to get into the darkest places of the country, even among those people who were farthest from any profession of faith. Yet this was not because I could not endure the light, for I was not afraid to show my gospel to anyone, but because I found that my spirit leaned most toward awakening and converting work, and the Word that I carried leaned most that way also: “Yes, in this way I have aspired to preach the gospel where Christ was not known, so that I would not be building on someone else’s foundation” (Rom 15:20).

290. In my preaching I have really been in pain, and have, as it were, travailed to bring forth children to God; nor could I be satisfied unless some fruits appeared in my work. If I were fruitless, it did not matter who commended me; but if I were fruitful, I did not care who condemned me. I have thought of that word, “He who wins souls is wise” (Prov 11:30); and again, “Children are indeed a heritage from the Lord, and the fruit of the womb is His reward. Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are children born in one’s youth. Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. He will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate” (Ps 127:3–5).

291. It pleased me not at all to see people drink in opinions if they seemed ignorant of Jesus Christ and of the worth of their own salvation. Sound conviction for sin, especially for unbelief, and a heart set on fire to be saved by Christ, with strong longings after a truly sanctified soul: that was what delighted me; those were the souls I counted blessed.

292. But in this work, as in all others, I had my temptations attending me, and those of different kinds. At times I would be assaulted with great discouragement in it, fearing that I would not be able to speak a word at all to edification; no, that I would not be able to speak sense to the people. At such times such a strange faintness and weakness would seize upon my body that my legs have scarcely been able to carry me to the place of meeting.

293. At other times, again, when I have been preaching, I have been violently assaulted with thoughts of blasphemy, and strongly tempted to speak the words with my mouth before the congregation. At times, too, when I have begun to speak the Word with much clearness, evidence, and liberty of speech, I have yet, before the end of that opportunity, been so blinded, and so estranged from the things I had been speaking, and also so hampered in my speech, in my utterance before the people, that I have been as if I did not know or remember what I was doing, or as if my head had been in a bag the whole time of the service.

294. Again, at times when I have been about to preach on some sharp and searching portion of the Word, I have found the tempter suggest, “What, will you preach this? This condemns you yourself of this your own soul is guilty; so do not preach on it at all. Or if you do, then mince it in such a way as to make room for your own escape; lest instead of awakening others, you lay such guilt upon your own soul as you will never get out from under.”

295. But, I thank the Lord, I have been kept from consenting to these horrid suggestions, and have rather, like Samson, bowed myself with all my might to condemn sin and transgression wherever I found it, yes, even though by doing so I brought guilt upon my own conscience! “Let me die,” I thought, “with the Philistines” (Judg 16:29, 30), rather than deal corruptly with the blessed Word of God. “You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?” It is far better that you judge yourself, even by preaching plainly to others, than that you, to save yourself, imprison the truth in unrighteousness. Blessed be God for His help in this also.

296. I have also, while engaged in this blessed work of Christ, often been tempted to pride and liftings up of heart. And though I dare not say I have not been affected by this, yet truly the Lord, of His precious mercy, has so dealt with me that, for the most part, I have had little joy in giving way to such a thing. For it has been my everyday portion to be let into the evil of my own heart, and continually made to see such a multitude of corruptions and infirmities in it, that it has caused a hanging down of the head under all my gifts and attainments. I have felt this thorn in the flesh, the very mercy of God to me (2 Cor 12:7–9).

297. Along with this I have also had some notable place or other of the Word set before me, a word that contained some sharp and piercing sentence concerning the perishing of the soul in spite of gifts and abilities. For instance, this has been of great use to me: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal” (1 Cor 13:1, 2).

298. A tinkling cymbal is an instrument of music with which a skillful player can make such melodious and heart-inflaming music that all who hear him play can scarcely keep from dancing; and yet, behold, the cymbal has no life, nor does the music come from it, except by the art of him who plays on it. So then the instrument may at last come to nothing and perish, though in times past such music has been made upon it.

299. Just so I saw it was, and will be, with those who have gifts but lack saving grace. They are in the hand of Christ as the cymbal was in the hand of David; and as David could with the cymbal make such mirth in the service of God as to lift up the hearts of the worshipers, so Christ can use these gifted men to move the souls of His people in His church; yet when He has done all, He can hang them up as lifeless, though sounding, cymbals.

300. This consideration, therefore, together with some others, was for the most part like a maul on the head of pride and the desire of vainglory. “What,” I thought, “shall I be proud because I am a sounding brass? Is it so much to be a fiddle? Does not the least creature that has life have more of God in it than these?” Besides, I knew it was love that should never die, but these must cease and vanish. So I concluded that a little grace, a little love, a little of the true fear of God, is better than all these gifts. Yes, and I am fully convinced that it is possible for souls who can scarcely give a man an answer except with great confusion as to method, I say it is possible for them to have a thousand times more grace, and so to be more in the love and favor of the Lord, than some who, by virtue of the gift of knowledge, can express themselves like angels.

301. So I came to see that though gifts in themselves were good for the thing for which they are designed, namely, the edification of others, yet they are empty and without power to save the soul of him who has them, if they are alone. Nor are they, as such, any sign that a man’s state is happy, being only a dispensation of God to some, who must, when a little while more is over, give an account of their use or neglect of them to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.

302. This showed me, too, that gifts, being alone, were dangerous, not in themselves, but because of the evils that attend those who have them, namely, pride, desire of vainglory, self-conceit, etc., all of which were easily puffed up by the applause and commendation of every thoughtless Christian, to the danger of a poor creature’s falling into the condemnation of the devil.

303. I saw, therefore, that he who has gifts needs to be let into a sight of their nature, namely, that they come short of making him to be in a truly saved condition, lest he rest in them, and so fall short of the grace of God.

304. He also has cause to walk humbly with God, and to be little in his own eyes, and to remember also that his gifts are not his own, but the church’s; and that by them he is made a servant to the church; and he must also at last give an account of his stewardship to the Lord Jesus; and to give a good account will be a blessed thing.

305. Let all men therefore prize a little with the fear of the Lord. Gifts indeed are desirable, but yet great grace and small gifts are better than great gifts and no grace. It does not say, the Lord gives gifts and glory, but, the Lord gives grace and glory; and blessed is the one to whom the Lord gives grace, true grace, for that is a certain forerunner of glory.

306. But when Satan saw that his tempting and assaulting me in this way would not serve his purpose, namely, to overthrow my ministry and make it ineffectual as to its ends, then he tried another way, which was to stir up the minds of the ignorant and malicious to load me with slanders and reproaches. Now therefore I may say that whatever the devil could devise, and his instruments invent, was whirled up and down the country against me, thinking, as I said, that by that means they would make my ministry be abandoned.

307. So it began to be rumored up and down among the people that I was a witch, a Jesuit, a highwayman, and the like.

308. To all this I shall only say, God knows that I am innocent. But as for my accusers, let them prepare themselves to meet me before the tribunal of the Son of God, there to answer for all these things, with all the rest of their iniquities, unless God gives them repentance for them, for which I pray with all my heart.

309. But what was reported with the boldest confidence was that I had my mistresses, my whores, my bastards, yes, two wives at once, and the like. Now these slanders, with the others, I glory in, because they are only slanders, foolish or knavish lies and falsehoods cast upon me by the devil and his seed; and if I were not dealt with this wickedly by the world, I would lack one sign of a saint and child of God. “Blessed are you+ (said the Lord Jesus) when people insult you+, persecute you+, and falsely say all kinds of evil against you+ because of Me. Rejoice and be glad, because great is your+ reward in heaven; for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you+” (Matt 5:11, 12).

310. These things, therefore, on my own account, do not trouble me; no, not though they were twenty times more than they are. I have a good conscience; and whereas they speak evil of me as an evildoer, those who falsely accuse my good conduct in Christ will be ashamed.

311. So then, what shall I say to those who have bespattered me in this way? Shall I threaten them? Shall I scold them? Shall I flatter them? Shall I beg them to hold their tongues? No, not I. Were it not that these things make those who are their authors and abettors ripe for damnation, I would say to them, “Report it, because it will increase my glory.”

312. Therefore I bind these lies and slanders to me as an ornament. It belongs to my Christian profession to be vilified, slandered, reproached, and reviled; and since all this is nothing but lies and slanders, as my God and my conscience bear me witness, I rejoice in reproaches for Christ’s sake.

313. I also call on all these fools or knaves, who have thus made it any part of their business to affirm any of the things named above about me, namely, that I have been immoral with other women, or the like, when they have used their utmost endeavors and made the fullest inquiry they can, to prove truly against me that there is any woman in heaven, or earth, or hell who can say that I have at any time, in any place, by day or night, so much as attempted to be immoral with her. And do I speak this way to beg my enemies into a good opinion of me? No, not I. In this I will beg belief of no man; believe or disbelieve me in this, it is all one to me.

314. My foes have missed their mark in this shooting at me. I am not the man. I wish that they themselves were guiltless. If all the fornicators and adulterers in England were hanged by the neck till they were dead, John Bunyan, the object of their envy, would still be alive and well. I do not know whether there is such a thing as a woman breathing under the whole vault of heaven, except by their clothing, their children, or common report, except my wife.

315. And in this I wonder at the wisdom of God, that He made me shy of women from my first conversion until now. Those with whom I have been most intimately concerned know, and can bear me witness, that it is a rare thing to see me behave pleasantly toward a woman. The common greeting of women with a kiss I abhor; it is odious to me in whomever I see it. I cannot bear to be in their company alone. I seldom so much as touch a woman’s hand, for I think these things are not fitting for me. When I have seen good men kiss in greeting the women they have visited, or who have visited them, I have at times made my objection against it; and when they have answered that it was only a piece of courtesy, I have told them it is not a seemly sight. Some indeed have urged the holy kiss; but then I have asked why they made exceptions, why they kissed the most handsome and let the plain ones go. So, however praiseworthy such things have been in the eyes of others, they have been unseemly in my sight.

316. And now to wind up this matter, I call on not only men, but angels, to prove me guilty of having carnally to do with any woman except my wife. Nor am I afraid to do it a second time, knowing that in such a case it cannot offend the Lord to call God as a witness upon my soul that in these things I am innocent. Not that I have been kept this way because of any goodness in me more than in anyone else; but God has been merciful to me and has kept me; and I pray to Him that He will keep me still, not only from this, but from every evil way and work, and preserve me to His heavenly kingdom. Amen.

317. Now as Satan labored by reproaches and slanders to make me despised among my countrymen, so that, if possible, my preaching might be made of no effect, so there was added to this a long and tedious imprisonment, so that by it I might be frightened from my service for Christ, and the world terrified and made afraid to hear me preach. Of this I shall next give you a brief account.

A Brief Account of the Author’s Imprisonment

318. Having made profession of the glorious gospel of Christ a long time, and preached it for about five years, I was arrested at a meeting of good people in the country, among whom, had they let me alone, I would have preached that day. But they took me away from among them and brought me before a justice, who, after I had offered security for my appearing at the next sessions, still committed me to prison, because my sureties would not consent to be bound that I would preach no more to the people.

319. At the sessions after that, I was indicted as an upholder and maintainer of unlawful assemblies and conventicles, and for not conforming to the national worship of the Church of England. And after some discussion there with the justices, they took my plain dealing with them as a confession, as they called it, of the indictment, and sentenced me to perpetual banishment, because I refused to conform. So, being delivered up again into the jailers’ hands, I was taken back to prison, and have now lain there a full twelve years, waiting to see what God will allow these men to do with me.

320. In this condition I have continued with much contentment, through grace, but have met with many turnings and goings upon my heart, from the Lord, from Satan, and from my own corruptions. By all of them (glory be to Jesus Christ!) I have also received, among many things, much conviction, instruction, and understanding, of which I shall not discourse at large here; I will only give you, in a hint or two, a word that may stir up the godly to bless God and to pray for me, and also to take encouragement, should the case be their own, not to fear what man can do to them.

321. I never in all my life had so great an entrance into the Word of God as now. Those scriptures that I saw nothing in before are made in this place and state to shine upon me. Jesus Christ also was never more real and apparent than now; here I have seen Him and felt Him indeed. Oh, that word, “We have not preached to you+ cunningly devised fables” (2 Pet 1:16), and that one, “God raised Christ from the dead and gave Him glory, so that your+ faith and hope might be in God” (1 Pet 1:21), were blessed words to me in this my imprisoned condition.

322. These three or four scriptures also have been a great refreshment to me in this condition (John 14:1–4; 16:33; Col 3:3, 4; Heb 12:22–24). So at times, when I have been in the savor of them, I have been able to laugh at destruction, and to fear neither the horse nor his rider (Job 39:18). I have had sweet sights of the forgiveness of my sins in this place, and of my being with Jesus in another world. Oh, “Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, the myriads of angels, and God the Judge of all, and the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus” (Heb 12:22–24) have been sweet to me in this place. I have seen that here which I am persuaded I shall never, while in this world, be able to express. I have seen a truth in that scripture, “Though you+ have not seen Him, you+ love Him; and though you+ do not see Him now, you+ believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy” (1 Pet 1:8).

323. I never knew what it was for God to stand by me at all turns, and at every attempt of Satan to afflict me, etc., as I have found Him since I came in here. For as fears have presented themselves, so have supports and encouragements. Yes, when I have been startled, as it were, at nothing but my own shadow, yet God, being very tender toward me, has not allowed me to be harassed, but would strengthen me against it all with one scripture or another; so much so that I have often said, “Were it lawful, I could pray for greater trouble, for the sake of the greater comfort” (Eccl 7:14; 2 Cor 1:5).

324. Before I came to prison, I saw what was coming, and had two considerations especially warm upon my heart. The first was how to be able to endure, should my imprisonment be long and tedious; the second was how to be able to face death, should that be my portion here. For the first of these, that scripture (Col 1:11) was great instruction to me, namely, to pray to God “to be strengthened with all power according to His glorious might, for all patience and long-suffering with joy.” For no less than a whole year before I was imprisoned, I could seldom go to prayer without this sentence, or sweet petition, as it were thrusting itself into my mind and persuading me that if ever I was to go through long-suffering, I must have all patience, especially if I would endure it joyfully.

325. As to the second consideration, that saying was of great use to me, “But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” (2 Cor 1:9). By this scripture I was made to see that if ever I was to suffer rightly, I must first pass a sentence of death upon everything that can properly be called a thing of this life, even to reckon myself, my wife, my children, my health, my enjoyments, and all, as dead to me, and myself as dead to them.

326. The second was to live upon God who is invisible, as Paul said in another place; the way not to faint is to fix our eyes “not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal” (2 Cor 4:18). And so I reasoned with myself: If I provide only for a prison, then the whip comes unexpectedly, and so does the pillory. Again, if I provide only for these, then I am not fit for banishment. Further, if I conclude that banishment is the worst, then if death comes, I am taken by surprise. So I see that the best way to go through sufferings is to trust in God through Christ as touching the world to come; and as touching this world, to count the grave my house, to make my bed in darkness, to say to corruption, “You are my father,” and to the worm, “You are my mother and sister”: that is, to make these things familiar to me.

327. But in spite of these helps, I found myself a man, and beset with infirmities. The parting with my wife and poor children has often been to me in this place like the pulling of the flesh from my bones; and that not only because I am somewhat too fond of these great mercies, but also because I would often call to mind the many hardships, miseries, and needs that my poor family was likely to meet with should I be taken from them, especially my poor blind child, who lay nearer my heart than all I had besides. Oh, the thought of the hardship I thought my blind one might go under would break my heart to pieces.

328. “Poor child,” I thought, “what sorrow are you likely to have for your portion in this world! You must be beaten, must beg, suffer hunger, cold, nakedness, and a thousand calamities, though I cannot now endure that the wind should blow upon you.” But yet, recalling myself, I thought, “I must venture you+ all with God, though it cuts to the quick to leave you+.” Oh, I saw that in this condition I was like a man who was pulling down his house upon the head of his wife and children; yet I thought, “I must do it, I must do it.” And now I thought of those two milk cows that were to carry the ark of God into another country and leave their calves behind them (1 Sam 6:10–12).

329. But what helped me in this temptation was various considerations, of which I will name three in particular here. The first was the consideration of these two scriptures: “Leave your fatherless children; I will preserve their lives. Let your widows trust in Me.” And again, “The Lord said: ‘Surely it will go well with your remnant; surely I will cause the enemy to treat you well in the time of evil’” (Jer 49:11; 15:11).

330. I had also this consideration: that if I should now venture all for God, I bound God to take care of my concerns; but if I forsook Him and His ways for fear of any trouble that might come to me or mine, then I would not only prove my profession false, but would also count my concerns not so safe if left at God’s feet, while I stood to and for His name, as they would be if they were under my own care, though with the denial of the way of God. This was a smarting consideration, and was like spurs to my flesh. That scripture also greatly helped to fasten it more upon me, where Christ prays against Judas that God would frustrate him in all his selfish thoughts, which moved him to sell his master. Please read it soberly (Ps 109:6–20).

331. I had also another consideration, and that was the dread of the torments of hell, which I was sure those must share in who for fear of the cross shrink from their profession of Christ, His words and laws, before the sons of men. I thought also of the glory that He had prepared for those who in faith, and love, and patience stood by His ways before them. These things, I say, have helped me when the thought of the misery that both I and mine might be exposed to for the sake of my profession has lain pinching on my mind.

332. When I have indeed imagined that I might be banished for my profession, then I have thought of that scripture, “They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were tempted, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated (the world was not worthy of them)” (Heb 11:37, 38), though people thought them too bad to dwell and abide among them. I have also thought of that saying, “In town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me” (Acts 20:23). I have truly thought that my soul and that word have at times reasoned together about the sore and sad state of a banished and exiled condition: how such men are exposed to hunger, to cold, to perils, to nakedness, to enemies, and a thousand calamities; and at last, it may be, to die in a ditch like a poor, forlorn, and desolate sheep. But I thank God that so far I have not been moved by these most delicate reasonings, but have rather, by them, more commended my heart to God.

333. I will tell you of a pretty business. I was once, above all the rest, in a very sad and low condition for many weeks; at which time also, being only a young prisoner and not acquainted with the laws, I had this lying heavily upon my spirit: that my imprisonment might end at the gallows, for all that I could tell. Now therefore Satan pressed hard upon me, to put me out of heart, by suggesting this to me: “But what if, when you come indeed to die, you should be in this condition, that is, not to savor the things of God, nor to have any evidence upon your soul for a better state hereafter?” For indeed at that time all the things of God were hidden from my soul.

334. So when I first began to think of this, it was a great trouble to me; for I thought to myself that in the condition I was now in, I was not fit to die, nor indeed did I think I could, if I should be called to it. Besides, I thought to myself, if I should make a scrambling shift to clamber up the ladder, I would yet, either with quaking or other symptoms of fainting, give occasion to the enemy to reproach the way of God and His people for their timidity. This, therefore, lay with great trouble upon me, for it seemed to me I was ashamed to die with a pale face and tottering knees for such a cause as this.

335. So I prayed to God that He would comfort me, and give me strength to do and suffer what He should call me to; yet no comfort appeared, but all continued hidden. I was also at this time so really possessed with the thought of death that it was often as if I were on a ladder with the rope about my neck. Only this was some encouragement to me: I thought I might now have an opportunity to speak my last words to a multitude, which I thought would come to see me die. “And,” I thought, “if it must be so, if God will convert even one soul by my very last words, I shall not count my life thrown away or lost.”

336. But still all the things of God were kept out of my sight, and still the tempter followed me with, “But where must you go when you die? What will become of you? Where will you be found in another world? What evidence do you have for heaven and glory, and an inheritance among those who are sanctified?” So I was tossed for many weeks, and did not know what to do. At last this consideration fell with weight upon me, that it was for the word and way of God that I was in this condition; so I was bound not to flinch a hair’s breadth from it.

337. I thought also that God might choose whether He would give me comfort now or at the hour of death; but I was not therefore free to choose whether I would hold to my profession or not. I was bound, but He was free. Yes, it was my duty to stand by His word, whether He would ever look upon me or save me at the last. So, I thought, the point being so, I am for going on and venturing my eternal state with Christ, whether I have comfort here or not. “If God does not come in,” I thought, “I will leap off the ladder even blindfold into eternity, sink or swim, come heaven, come hell. Lord Jesus, if You will catch me, do; if not, I will venture for Your name.”

338. No sooner was I fixed upon this resolution than that word dropped upon me, “Does Job serve God for nothing?” It was as if the accuser had said, “Lord, Job is no upright man; he serves You for selfish ends. Have You not placed a hedge on every side around him? But stretch out Your hand and strike all that he has, and he will surely curse You to Your face.” “How now,” I thought, “is this the sign of an upright soul, to desire to serve God when all is taken from him? Is he a godly man who will serve God for nothing rather than give up? Blessed be God; then I hope I have an upright heart, for I am resolved, God giving me strength, never to deny my profession, though I have nothing at all for my pains.” And as I was considering this, that scripture was set before me (Ps 44:12–26).

339. Now my heart was full of comfort, for I hoped it was sincere. I would not have been without this trial for much. I am comforted every time I think of it, and I hope I shall bless God forever for the teaching I have had by it. I might relate many more of the dealings of God with me, but “these, out of the spoils won in battle, I have dedicated to maintain the house of God” (1 Chr 26:27).

The Conclusion

1. Of all the temptations that I ever met with in my life, to question the being of God and the truth of His gospel is the worst, and the worst to be borne. When this temptation comes, it takes away my belt from me and removes the foundation from under me. Oh, I have often thought of that word, “Have the belt of truth buckled around your+ waist”; and of that one, “If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?”

2. At times, when after committing sin I have looked for severe chastisement from the hand of God, the very next thing I have had from Him has been the revealing of His grace. At times, when I have been comforted, I have called myself a fool for sinking so under trouble. And then again, when I have been cast down, I thought I was not wise to give way to comfort as I did. With such strength and weight have both these been upon me.

3. I have wondered much at this one thing: that though God visits my soul with ever so blessed a revealing of Himself, yet I have found afterward that such hours have come upon me that I have been so filled with darkness in my spirit that I could not so much as once conceive what that God and that comfort was with which I had been refreshed.

4. I have at times seen more in a line of the Bible than I could well tell how to stand under, and yet at another time the whole Bible has been to me as dry as a stick; or rather, my heart has been so dead and dry toward it that I could not conceive the least dram of refreshment, though I have looked it all over.

5. Of all fears, those are best that are made by the blood of Christ; and of all joy, that is the sweetest which is mixed with mourning over Christ. Oh, it is a goodly thing to be on our knees, with Christ in our arms, before God. I hope I know something of these things.

6. I find to this day seven abominations in my heart: (1) Inclinings to unbelief. (2) Quickly forgetting the love and mercy that Christ shows. (3) A leaning to the works of the law. (4) Wanderings and coldness in prayer. (5) Forgetting to watch for what I pray for. (6) Being apt to murmur because I have no more, and yet ready to abuse what I have. (7) I can do none of the things which God commands me without my corruptions thrusting themselves in: “When I want to do good, evil is right there with me.”

7. These things I continually see and feel, and am afflicted and oppressed with; yet the wisdom of God orders them for my good. (1) They make me abhor myself. (2) They keep me from trusting my heart. (3) They convince me of the insufficiency of all inherent righteousness. (4) They show me the necessity of fleeing to Jesus. (5) They press me to pray to God. (6) They show me the need I have to watch and be sober. (7) And they provoke me to pray to God, through Christ, to help me and carry me through this world. Amen.
